# PREFACE.

Although we are no longer in those unhappy centuries when nearly the entire world was plunged into the shadows of Idolatry, one can hardly do without a knowledge of the history of the Gods and the fables of <term>Paganism</term> <note>original: Paganisme; here referring to the polytheistic religions of the ancient world</note>. <term>Mythology</term> <note>original: Mythologie</note>, which teaches us to understand these fables and these gods, constitutes too significant a part of <term>Belles-Lettres</term> <note>original: Belles-Lettres; literally "fine letters," referring to the study of literature and the humanities</note> for it to be neglected. In fact, we read the works of the Greeks and Romans daily, especially those of their poets, whom it would often be very difficult to understand if one did not know the fables to which they make constant allusion.

Moreover, everything conspires to remind us of these ancient fictions: statues, bas-reliefs, and monuments of every kind. Indeed, what fills the books of <term>antiquarians</term> <note>original: Antiquaires; scholars who studied ancient artifacts and history</note> and the <term>cabinets of curiosities</term> <note>original: Cabinets des Curieux; private collections of notable objects, often precursors to modern museums</note> but images of <term>divinities</term> <note>original: Divinités</note>, sacrificial instruments, and everything that remains to us of ancient Paganism? Our galleries, our ceilings, our paintings, our statues—

<header>PREFACE.</header>

...ceaselessly represent the same objects to us; and as if <term>sacred and profane history</term> <note>original: l'Hiſtoire ſainte & profane; "sacred" refers to Biblical history, while "profane" refers to secular or non-biblical ancient history</note> did not provide enough interesting facts capable of inspiring virtuous sentiments in us, we borrow our subjects from <term>Fable</term> <note>original: la Fable; a term used in this period to refer to the collection of ancient myths and legends</note>, especially in our dramatic poetry.

Our theaters resound every day with the complaints of <term>Iphigenia</term> and <term>Andromache</term>, the rages of <term>Orestes</term>, and the outbursts of <term>Achilles</term> and <term>Clytemnestra</term> <note>Characters from Greek tragedy: Iphigenia was sacrificed by her father; Andromache was the widow of Hector; Orestes avenged his father Agamemnon; Achilles was the greatest Greek warrior; Clytemnestra was the wife and murderer of Agamemnon</note>; and let us not blush to admit it: we always view these heroes and heroines upon our stage with a renewed pleasure, while we often find it difficult to endure other characters more suited to excite a noble emulation within us.

It is therefore useful, and even in some sense necessary, to know Mythology; thus we see that those who are ignorant of it are considered to be lacking in education and the most necessary enlightenment for a <term>man of letters</term> <note>original: homme de Lettres; a person of broad scholarly and literary learning</note>. But when one comes to consider that the Fables are not pure fictions, as I prove at the beginning of this work; that they have a real relationship with the history of the first centuries; that they contain significant events; and that most of the Gods were actually men whose history forms part of that of the peoples who worshipped them—then Mythology becomes a more important object, and at the same time, more worthy of our curiosity.

It is this historical foundation, hidden beneath the cloak of Fable, which was the principal object of my research when I began to apply myself to the study of Mythology; and the public favorably received the *Explanation*...

...Historical [Explanation] of Fables, which was the first essay I produced on this subject (1); but at the same time, the public seemed to desire a more extensive and more profound Mythology. This work, as enlightened people have often told me, is missing from our language; since, without mentioning the outdated style of those we have in French on this subject, one finds nothing systematic in them. The Fables are not traced back to any source or any specific time; the origin of the Gods is not developed there; one does not distinguish between those Gods who were often the same under different names; finally, if one finds some traces of History, they are drowned in a mass of arbitrary Allegories and Moralities (2).

Moreover, the authors of these Mythologies, deprived of the discoveries of the scholars who have come since, followed unreliable guides; and today we are in a better position than they were to treat this subject. What light indeed have the <term>Meziriacs</term>, the <term>Bocharts</term>, the <term>Vossiuses</term>, and several others not shed upon it? <note>Claude-Gaspard Bachet de Méziriac, Samuel Bochart, and Gerardus Vossius were 17th-century polymaths whose work in philology, geography, and theology helped provide a historical and linguistic context for ancient myths</note> And if these learned men had explained all the Fables as they explained those that happened to have some connection with the subjects they had undertaken to clarify, we would not need a new Mythology.

To satisfy what was expected of me, I formed the design for the work I am presenting today. # PREFACE.

<margin>(*) Mr. Fourmont the elder <note>Étienne Fourmont (1683–1745), a renowned French orientalist and member of the Academy of Inscriptions, known for his vast knowledge of ancient and Eastern languages.</note>.</margin>

I had already benefited greatly in my *Historical Explanation* <note>original: "Explication Historique"; referring to his earlier work, *The History of Fables Explained by History*</note> from the discoveries made by the scholars of the last century, and it will be easy to see in this *Mythology* that I have read them again with renewed care; I have also made the same use of several other books related to my subject that have appeared since. I have particularly consulted the *Critical Reflections on Ancient Peoples* <note>original: "Réflexions critiques sur les anciens Peuples"; a work by Étienne Fourmont published in 1735</note>, a profound work in which the Author (*), for whom the learned languages hold no secrets, demonstrates throughout as much sagacity as knowledge. Indeed, whether he undertakes to prove the authenticity of a precious fragment in a way that it can no longer be contested, or whether he develops the origin of ancient peoples, or finally, whether he traces most Fables back to their primary source, it is always with an uncommon level of erudition, and often through discoveries that had escaped other scholars.

Guided, moreover, in my research by the insights of a Company <note>original: "Compagnie"; referring to the *Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres*, a French learned society devoted to the humanities</note> in which the most profound erudition is combined with the most judicious criticism, I have equally benefited from the valuable collection of its works and from the learned conversations that fill certain moments of its meetings.

With these aids, and through a study continued for several years, I finally believed myself to be in a position to present this *Mythology*; and to make it accessible to everyone, I have avoided, as much as I could, those thorny discussions which usually discourage the majority of readers, so as to say about each subject only what there is...

# P R E F A C E.

...[is] most useful and most interesting; and it will be clearly seen that often my consideration for them <note>The author refers here to his readers, prioritizing their understanding over a display of his own learning.</note> has been dearer to me than my own reputation; for it is no small thing for an author to suppress points of erudition that he has at hand, and which would cost him no more than the effort to transcribe.

This, then, is the method I have followed. When I use the testimony of an Author, I usually report their words and provide a translation; and when such a translation is missing, the discourse that precedes or follows the quotation makes its meaning clear enough. I take care, as much as possible, to cite the oldest authors before those who followed later; thus **Homer** and **Hesiod** among the Poets, and **Herodotus** and some others among the Historians, are always preferred over those who came after them. 

It is not that I neglect these latter ones: they may have consulted Traditions or Works that still existed in their time; and the earliest writers certainly did not say everything: it is only a matter of the preference I give to some over others. The Poets, who have transmitted so many fictions to us, are nonetheless—whatever may be said of them—the first keepers of the ancient Traditions of Greece, and its first Historians, since writing in **Prose** began there only very late.

To the Poets and Historians I have sometimes added Medals <term>Médailles: In the eighteenth century, this term was commonly used to refer to ancient coins, which were studied as historical evidence alongside texts.</term> and Inscriptions, because these are monuments that attest to ancient Tradition.

Regarding the **Moderns** who have worked on this subject, I limit myself to report—

...report their sentiment in general, and those of their proofs which appeared to me most conclusive. When they have written specific **Dissertations** <note>Formal academic treatises or essays popular in the 18th century.</note> on these same subjects, I take the substance of them, and I refer to the **Dissertations** themselves those who might have the curiosity to read them.

Furthermore, I do not believe I have anything to reproach myself for regarding the use of others' discoveries without at least doing them the justice of naming them. The crime of <term>Plagiarism</term> <note>The act of taking someone else's work or ideas and passing them off as one's own.</note> has always seemed an odious crime to me; and who would be a greater plagiarist than I, if I had not carefully indicated the sources from which I have drawn, and from which any Author who produces a Work similar to mine must necessarily draw? A Work which, in truth, brings less honor than a new system: but which at the same time is almost always more useful to the Public. Those who take the trouble to read the first Chapter of this **Mythology**, which is a continuation of this Preface, will see how many baseless suppositions those who wanted to reduce the **Fables** <note>Ancient myths or stories.</note> to a general system have exposed themselves to. For after all, if every People has had its fictions, they are rather the fruit of the human spirit—always inclined toward the marvelous—than the result of a concerted project.

My design in this Work is to prove that despite all the ornaments that accompany the **Fables**, it is not difficult to see that they contain a portion of the History of the earliest times, and that **Allegory** and **Morality** were not the primary objective of those who invented them; and far from having changed my mind, I have been further confirmed in it by new studies. # P R E F A C E.

...tain <margin>(1) See the 1st Chapter.</margin> some particular fictions where one would search in vain for any historical traits (1): but in general, almost all of them have some connection to history, or are linked to events authorized by everything that is most respectable in **Antiquity** <note>The period of ancient history, particularly Greek and Roman history and culture.</note>.

In the past, **Mythologists** <note>Those who study and interpret myths.</note> believed they had penetrated the meaning of a **Fable** <note>A myth or legendary story; in this period, "fable" was the standard term for Greco-Roman mythology.</note> once they had succeeded in drawing from it some allegory or moral lesson; and this is essentially what all their explanations amounted to. Today, the **Scholars**—persuaded that **Fables** hide the History of the times following the **Deluge** <note>The Great Flood, traditionally referring to the biblical flood of Noah, which 18th-century scholars used as a primary chronological marker.</note> beneath ingenious coverings—have applied themselves to lifting the mysterious veil that hid the truths they contain from short-sighted eyes.

There are times favorable to certain opinions, and that of the historical truth within **Fables** has so thoroughly gained the upper hand that one must henceforth either gracefully renounce finding any reasonable meaning in them at all, or else relate them to **History**.

However, one can raise an objection against this opinion that at first seems very solid: How can we trace back to **History** what the **Greeks**, for example, say about their Gods, since these Gods lived in the eras they themselves call "unknown"? What **History** can be drawn from an "unknown" time—a time which would no longer be unknown if we had some knowledge of it?

To be better acquainted with this difficulty, one must recall the famous division made by **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), a Roman scholar and writer whose chronological divisions of history were highly influential.</note>, who divided time into **unknown times**, **fabulous times**, and **historical times**. The first category included everything that happened in the world until the time of **Ogyges** <note>A legendary king of Attica or Boeotia; his reign was often cited by ancients as the furthest point back that Greek memory could reach.</note>; and it was in this interval that lived

<meta>This page continues the author's response to an objection regarding the chronology of "unknown times." He is addressing the division of history into the eras of Gods, Heroes, and Men, as proposed by ancient writers like Varro.</meta>

->### PREFACE.<-

...the Gods. The second [period] extended from **Ogygés** <note>A legendary primordial king of early Greece; his name was synonymous with "primeval."</note> until the re-establishment of the **Olympiads** <note>The four-year cycles used by the Greeks to track time, starting traditionally in 776 BCE.</note>; and it was in this second space of time that the **Heroes** and **Demi-Gods** had appeared. Finally, with the **Olympiads**, historical times began.

To respond to this difficulty, I say:

1. That this division only concerned the **Greeks**; for those times which they called "unknown" were not so for **Asia** nor for **Egypt**, where there were powerful **Monarchies**, and a system of **Religion** established since the most remote ages. The **Greeks** did not yet exist—or at least they were a rude and wandering people, without laws, without politeness <note>In the 18th century, "politeness" referred to the refinement of a civilized society.</note>, and almost without **Religion**—at the time when the Peoples of the **East** enjoyed all the advantages provided by the **Arts** and **Sciences**.

2. For this objection to have any force, it would be necessary that these **Gods**, whose **History** one undertakes to provide, were **Greek** by origin; for one might then say that the **Greeks**, who knew nothing certain of the times in which they claimed [the Gods] had lived, could not have transmitted their **History** to posterity: but these **Gods** were foreign to them. The **Colonies** that came at different times from **Egypt** and **Phoenicia** <note>A maritime civilization in the Levant (modern Lebanon/Syria) known for spreading their alphabet and culture.</note> to settle in **Greece** brought the **Religion** and the **Gods** of their country there. This is a truth that one cannot deny; and **Herodotus** <note>The 5th-century BCE Greek historian often called the "Father of History."</note>, informed about the **Religion** of the **Egyptians** by their very Priests, says so positively. The **Gods** of the **Greeks** were therefore originally from **Egypt** and **Phoenicia**, and had been the object of religious worship in these two Countries long before the **Colonies** of which I speak had arrived in...

...that they had for the marvelous, even in **Histories** that were better known and more recent; how would they have respected the truth when it came to these distant times, in which it was not easy to prove them wrong?

Let us shed further light on this answer. The **Greeks** were instructed by the peoples of the **Orient**, and particularly by the **Egyptians**, regarding the **History of the Gods** who had lived during the period of time that **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar, who categorized history into the unknown, the fabulous, and the historical.</note> called the *unknown times*. **Cadmus** <note>The legendary Phoenician prince who founded Thebes and is credited with bringing the alphabet to Greece.</note> taught them the use of **Letters**, and enabled them to write the **History** of their **Heroes** themselves—that is to say, the history of the **fabulous times**. The **Works** that contained this history apparently still existed in the time of **Hesiod** and **Homer** <note>The primary epic poets of ancient Greece, traditionally dated to the 8th century BC.</note>, who derived the substance of their **Poems** from them, or at least drew it from a tradition that was still quite recent. I am convinced that these **Poems** caused the loss of most other older **Works**; for it has happened more than once that a good book has caused people to forget, and finally caused the disappearance of those which preceded it. 

But as **Homer** and **Hesiod** had not employed all the traditions that were received in their time, the other **Poets** who came after them made use of what remained; and this is why we find such different accounts in **Sophocles**, in **Euripides** <note>Two of the three great Athenian tragedians whose plays often featured varying versions of myths.</note>, and in the other **Tragic writers**. As for the **Authors** who later collected the **History** of these ancient events in **Prose**, such as **Apollodorus** <note>An Athenian scholar whose "Library" is a primary source for Greek myths.</note>, **Diodorus** <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian known for his monumental universal history, the "Bibliotheca historica."</note>, and several others, they drew what they recount either from this same tradition, or from the **Works** that still existed in their time, and which had themselves been composed based on others even more ancient.

Finally, I speak of the **Heroes** and **Demi-Gods**: and to provide a more specific knowledge of them, I delve into the depths of the **Ancient History of Greece**, that of the peoples who inhabited it, and all the events that made it famous; and I have concluded this Work with an explanation of the **Fables** <note>In this context, "fables" refers to the mythological stories, allegories, and poetic inventions of the ancient world.</note> which have no connection to the facts reported throughout the Volumes.

At the beginning of each Volume, one finds a **Table of Chapters**, which describes in greater detail all the subjects I cover, and at the end of the final volume, a **General Index** <note>original: "Table générale"</note>, which I have endeavored to make as useful as possible.

Some people might have wished that I had included **Illustrations of the Gods** <note>original: "Figures des Dieux"</note> in this Work, and I admit they would have made it easier to understand and would often have spared me from giving lengthy descriptions; but besides the fact that they would have greatly increased the cost, I believed it sufficient to point out the Books where they may be found—books which today are quite widely distributed and well known.

## CHAPTER I.

### General Reflections on Mythology.

**K**nowledge of Mythology is certainly not so necessary today as it seemed to the early Fathers of the Church, who had undertaken to establish the Christian Religion upon the ruins of Idolatry, or to defend this same Religion through learned apologies <note>In this context, "apologies" refers to formal written defenses of a doctrine or belief, from the Greek *apologia*.</note> against the slanders being published against it. They were required to penetrate the most hidden mysteries of Paganism to reveal all its horrors; and they had to respond to subtle Philosophers who, in order to diminish the absurdity of the worship for which they were being criticized, had recourse to allegorical explanations which seemed to give a reasonable sense to even the most impious practices. From this came the Works of Porphyry, Iamblichus, Proclus, Plotinus, and several other Platonic Philosophers. From this also came the Apologies of the Fathers of the first centuries: St. Justin, Arnobius, Theodoret, Lactantius, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, St. Augustine, etc.

<term>Mythology: The study of myths and fables, particularly those of the Greeks and Romans.</term>
<term>Paganism: A term used by early Christians to describe the polytheistic religions of the ancient world.</term>
<term>Idolatry: The worship of idols or images as gods.</term>
<term>Platonic Philosophers: Followers of Plato’s teachings who, in later centuries (Neoplatonists), often tried to harmonize ancient myths with philosophical truths.</term>
<term>Porphyry: A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who was a significant opponent of early Christianity.</term>
<term>Iamblichus: A student of Porphyry and a philosopher who defended theurgy and traditional pagan rituals.</term>
<term>Proclus: One of the last major Greek philosophers, who wrote extensively on Plato and theology.</term>
<term>Plotinus: The founder of Neoplatonism, whose philosophical system influenced both later paganism and Christian theology.</term>
<term>St. Justin: Justin Martyr, an early Christian apologist who defended the faith to the Roman Emperor.</term>
<term>Arnobius: An early Christian writer known for his work "Against the Pagans."</term>
<term>Theodoret: A bishop and theologian who wrote on the "Cure of Greek Maladies," comparing Christianity to pagan philosophy.</term>
<term>Lactantius: A Christian advisor to Constantine, often called the "Christian Cicero" for his eloquent Latin style.</term>
<term>Clement of Alexandria: A teacher who sought to demonstrate how Greek philosophy could lead to Christian truth.</term>
<term>Tertullian: A prolific early Christian author from Carthage, famous for his rigorous defenses of the faith.</term>
<term>St. Augustine: The influential Bishop of Hippo, whose "City of God" provided a definitive critique of Roman paganism.</term>

<summary>This chapter explains that while mythology is no longer a religious threat, it was once a vital field of study for early Church Fathers who needed to dismantle pagan arguments and allegories.</summary>
<keywords>early Church Fathers, Christian Apologists, Neoplatonism, allegorical interpretation, Paganism, religious history</keywords>

Truth has finally triumphed over error; and if some remnants of ancient superstitions are still found among coarse and ignorant nations, it is not Religion that authorizes them; they have even disappeared as the world has become more enlightened.

I dare, however, to assert that the knowledge of this same Mythology is still very useful. It forms a part of *Literature* <note>original: "Belles-Lettres"</note>, and it serves infinitely in the understanding of the **Poets** and certain **Historians** who recount the ancient **Fables**, or who make constant allusions to them. One finds these Fables everywhere, and they still provide the subject for most of our dramatic or lyrical pieces and our paintings. Now, one must agree: 1st. That when one reads the Poets and finds these ancient fictions, which they knew how to employ with such art, one feels a keen curiosity to penetrate their meaning. 2nd. That successful explanations, freed from the clutter of **allegories** and **moralizing** which made up the entire foundation of our first Mythologists, shed a great light on these ancient Authors and serve to help us understand them with greater ease. These are the just boundaries within which I

<term>Fables: In this context, the traditional stories or myths of antiquity.</term>
<term>Allegories: Stories or images where the characters and events represent abstract ideas or moral principles.</term>

I am well aware that we possess a great number of **Works** on this subject, both ancient and modern; I nevertheless believed it was still necessary to provide one that was both more methodical and more complete than those we currently have. What I am about to say regarding those I know will prove what I have just asserted, after I have in good faith exhorted those who have some talent for this matter to work upon it seriously. For one would be mistaken to imagine that I believe I have exhausted the subject, and one would know me poorly if they judged me capable of that base jealousy held against those who bring the scythe into a harvest <note>A metaphor for intellectual territoriality; the author welcomes other scholars to "harvest" the same field of knowledge.</note> that one seems to have reserved for oneself: the field that I have cultivated for so many years is vast enough to receive several workers.

# ARTICLE THE FIRST.

## *What a Mythologist’s knowledge ought to consist of.*

By **Mythology**, I mean the knowledge of **Fable**, and at the same time of the **Pagan Religion**, its mysteries, its ceremonies, and the worship with which it honored its false Divinities.

It is easily understood that to truly know Fable, one must have carefully read the Poets—Homer and Hesiod—and especially the Tragedians who drew the subjects of their poems from them, as well as those who compiled collections of them: in verse, like Ovid; in prose, like Antoninus Liberalis <note>A Greek grammarian of the 2nd century AD known for his collection of transformation myths.</note>, Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BC who attempted a universal history.</note>, Apollodorus <note>Traditional author of the *Library*, a massive compendium of Greek myths and hero legends.</note>, Hyginus <note>Presumed author of the *Fabulae*, a fundamental handbook of Roman and Greek mythology.</note>, and several others.

Knowing Fable <note>In this context, "Fable" refers specifically to the body of mythological stories and legends.</note> thoroughly is, strictly speaking, only the first step for a Mythologist. Since Fables contain several layers of meaning, and serve as various coverings under which the Ancients concealed many truths, those who have set out to explain them have ventured into different

### Explanation by History, Book I, Chapter I.

...thologists, at their head stands Natalis Comes <note>Natale Conti (1520–1582), an Italian scholar whose *Mythologiae* was the standard handbook of classical mythology in late Renaissance Europe.</note>, a learned author who might have spared us the need to work on this same subject, if—being too biased toward the allegorical and moral meanings of the Fables—he had applied himself a little more to investigating only their history. The *Mythology* of Cartari <note>Vincenzo Cartari, author of *Le Immagini de i Dei de gli Antichi* (1556), which focused on how the gods were depicted in art.</note>, continued by du Verdier, contains nothing very instructive or well-organized. The work of Lilio Giraldi <note>Lilio Gregorio Giraldi (1479–1552), author of *De deis gentium*, a scholarly and systematic catalog of pagan deities.</note> is very good for what it contains; however, beyond the fact that it does not cover every subject that should be included in a Mythology, he neglected the history hidden within these ancient fictions. Its best feature is the list of surnames for the gods he discusses, which appears to have been compiled with great care, although he often neglected to provide the explanations for these names. 

The commentary by Vigenère <note>Blaise de Vigenère (1523–1596), a French diplomat and translator.</note> on the *Images* of Philostratus <note>Philostratus the Elder (3rd century AD); his *Imagines* describes a series of paintings in a Neapolitan gallery.</note> is very learned, but too heavily mixed with natural philosophy <note>original: "Physique"</note> and morality, and written in a language that is no longer spoken <note>The author refers to the archaic 16th-century French used by Vigenère, which felt dated by the 18th century.</note>.

## ARTICLE II.

->*The pitfalls a Mythologist must avoid.*<-

After having addressed the preliminary knowledge that a mythologist must acquire, I shall now show him the pitfalls he must avoid regarding the various systems that have been devised to explain <term>Fables</term> <note>In this period, "Fables" was the standard term for what we now call myths or classical mythology.</note>; for as there is not one among them that satisfies every difficulty, there are no general rules that can serve on every occasion. They argued these stories represented, above all, the various productions of **secondary causes** <note>In philosophical terms, "secondary causes" are the laws of nature or celestial beings through which a primary creator acts upon the world.</note>, animated by the same spirit that had developed them and drawn them from the chaos in which they were once confounded. # Mythology & the Fables

...because the **Fables** <note>In this period, "Fables" refers specifically to the myths of the ancient world, often viewed as stories requiring decoding.</note> were never a deliberate work, nor composed to form a unified whole; nevertheless, this system explains the allegories they sometimes contain in a very ingenious manner. **Plato** himself, the Master of the **Philosophers** who formed this system, had explained some of them based on this principle.

Some **Scholars** <note>original: "Sçavans"</note> of the last century took another path to penetrate the meaning of the Fables. **Father Kircher** <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit scholar famous for his wide-ranging interests and his attempts—now known to be incorrect—to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs before the discovery of the Rosetta Stone.</note> claimed to find the solution in the explanation of **Hieroglyphs**, or the sacred language of the **Egyptians**; this claim is generally false, and by no means certain, given the little knowledge we have of this mysterious language, and because, in fact, not all Fables originate from **Egypt**.

However, as this country was among the first populated, and shortly after the dispersion of the sons of **Noah**, and since the Fables appear as ancient as this first separation—given that the **Idolatry** with which they are linked began then—nothing is more useful for understanding them, and for enabling the **Mythologist** to explain them, than the knowledge of the **Religion** and **Ceremonies** of this ancient People;

# Mythology & the Fables

The system of those who relate all Fables to the Holy Scriptures <note>The Bible, particularly the Old Testament.</note> misunderstood, and to corrupted traditions, is certainly false when it is taken as a general rule. There are an infinite number of things in Fables that have no relation to the facts found in the Holy Books; which, moreover, were preserved by a People <note>The Jewish/Hebrew people.</note> jealous of their Religion, not at all communicative, much despised, and little known before the conquests of *Alexander* <note>Alexander the Great (356–323 BCE), whose conquests facilitated the first major cultural exchange between the Greek and Judean worlds.</note>. But, to say here what I think on this subject, there is not one of the Authors I have just named who has not gone too far. It is dangerous to let oneself be dazzled by the first glimmers of resemblance that strike us, and it is a reef upon which many learned men have shipwrecked. # Mythology and Fables

Similarly, although it is certain that truth did not emerge from the heart of error, but rather that truth itself—when misunderstood—produced the great number of Fables <note>In this context, "Fables" refers to the myths, legends, and "false" religions of antiquity.</note> that seduced almost the entire world for many centuries; and that consequently, those who have sought to discover this ancient truth within the depths of error are worthy of praise, one cannot help but blame them for wanting to push their conjectures too far. 

For example, they have claimed that traces of the mystery of the Trinity could be found in the works of Plato—as Saint Justin, Eusebius, Clement of Alexandria, and several others imagined <note>These early Christian "Church Fathers" sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine, arguing that Plato had a primitive understanding of the nature of God.</note>; or in the hieroglyphic figures of the *Isiac Table* <note>The *Tabula Bembina* or Isiac Table: an elaborate bronze tablet of Egyptian style which sparked much debate among 17th-century scholars regarding its meaning.</note>, as others have believed; or in the Divinities of the ancient Germans, as Cluverius <note>Philipp Cluverius (1580–1623), a celebrated geographer and historian.</note> proposed; or in the three principal Gods of the East Indies: Brahma, Vishnu, and Rudra <note>original: "Routren." This refers to the Hindu Trimurti, typically Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva (Rudra).</note>; or in the three-headed idol of Japan; or in that of Peru called *Tanga-Tanga*—a name which, according to Acosta <note>José de Acosta (1540–1600), a Jesuit missionary and author of the *Natural and Moral History of the Indies*.</note>, means *one in three, or three in one* <note>original: "un en trois, ou trois en un"</note>. To do this is a desire to distinguish oneself through learned eccentricities at the expense of that very truth.

<header>Mythology & Fables</header>

The approach that traces **Fables** back to **Ancient History**—though distorted by the **Poets**, who were the first Historians—seems to be the most popular today. I have followed it myself, encouraged by the success of several **Scholars** <note>original: "Sçavans"</note> of the last century who so successfully explained certain specific Fables. However, this system would also have its drawbacks if one tried to relate everything generally to History, since it is certain that there are Fables which are nothing but pure allegories: representing either some virtue, some vice, or even the productions of nature.

There are others whose foundation is historical, although allegory was used to present them to us, as in the fable of the **children of Niobe** <note>In Greek myth, Niobe boasted of her fourteen children, insulting the goddess Leto; as punishment, Leto’s children Apollo and Diana killed all of Niobe's offspring.</note>, who perished in the **plague** <note>original: "contagion"</note> that afflicted the city of **Thebes**. It is said poetically that they were killed by **Apollo** and **Diana** because sudden deaths and those caused by the plague were attributed to Apollo for men, and to Diana for women, as is seen in a hundred places in **Homer** <note>The ancient Greek author of the Iliad and the Odyssey.</note>. This was because people believed that the plague was the result of the influences of the **Sun** and the **Moon**, signified by the **arrows** of these two Divinities.

I do not claim that a **Fable** <note>In this context, "Fable" refers to a mythological story or legend.</note> was not yet invented in the time of these ancient **Poets** just because they do not speak of it. They did not have the opportunity nor the intention to mention them all; here is how I understand it. When they relate a **Fable**, whatever they do not report seems to have been invented only after their time. 

Thus, for example, **Hesiod** <note>An early Greek poet (c. 700 BCE) whose work serves as a primary source for Greek mythology.</note> says that **Jason** had a son by **Medea** named **Medus**, and says nothing more; from this I conclude that it was only after him that someone added to this **Fable** the claim that this **Medus** was the father of the **Medes** <note>The Medes were an ancient Iranian people. For one dares to assert here that nothing will ever be raised against the brotherhood of the three Titan Princes that is stronger than the arguments already used to establish it.

# Explanation by History, Book I, Chapter II

[O]cean is the father of the Rivers, that the **Sirens** are daughters of **Achelous**, <note>Achelous was the god of the largest river in Greece; his daughters, the Sirens, were often interpreted as symbols of the dangers of the sea or seductive music.</note> etc., are these not evident allegories of **Physics**? <note>In this context, "Physics" refers to the study of the natural world and the elements, rather than the modern laboratory science.</note> I admit it; but that is not the ancient state of the **Fables**. In that state, **Bacchus** is regarded as a conquering Prince; **Jupiter** as a King of **Crete** famous for his conquests; **Ceres** as a Queen of **Sicily** who taught **Agriculture** to her People; and so with the others. It was only later that the idea of the **Elements** and of all nature was attached to these ancient **Fables**. This proves only that many allegories have been mixed into them, which no one denies; and it is undoubtedly this which renders them so difficult to explain, the **Poets** passing suddenly from **History** to **Physics**. 

Thus, one should regard these allegories as metaphors and figurative expressions which were added to highlight the characters of the persons of whom one wishes to speak. Thus, one should view these allegories as metaphors and figurative expressions that were added to highlight the character of the individuals being discussed. # Mythology & Fables

Strabo’s judicious remark concerning the voyages of **Ulysses** <note>original: "Ulyffe"</note>—into which **Homer** mixed so many **Fables**—strongly confirms what has just been stated.

> "By keeping ancient **History** before our eyes," says this Author, "we must examine on this footing what is said by those who maintain that **Ulysses** was carried into the seas of Italy and Sicily, as **Homer** has said, and those who deny it. For these two opinions each have their merits and flaws, and one can be correct while being mistaken on both sides. One is correct if one believes that **Homer**, convinced that **Ulysses** had been carried to all these locations, took a very real subject as the foundation for his **Fable**; but that he treated it as a **Poet**, that is to say, by blending in fiction. For one finds in these seas vestiges of his voyages; yet one is mistaken if one takes for a detailed **History** all the rest of the fiction—such as his Ocean, his Underworlds <note>original: "Enfers"; referring to the Odyssey's Book XI where Ulysses visits the spirits of the dead</note>, his **Metamorphoses**, the horrible figure of **Scylla**, that of the **Cyclops**, and the rest. He who would maintain all these points as so many historical truths would no more deserve to be refuted than he who would [deny] that **Ulysses** truly arrived in **Ithaca** <note>original: "Ithaca"; the hero's home island. The author implies it is just as foolish to believe in monsters as it is to be so skeptical that one denies the basic historical fact of the journey itself.</note>."

### Explanation by History: Book I, Chapter II. 47

"...in the manner that **Homer** recounted it."

Both of these opinions are ridiculous; one must hold the middle ground and disentangle what is historical from the ornaments of fiction. Thus, to judge correctly on this subject, one must look at the foundation of **Fables** <note>In this context, "Fables" refers to the myths and legends of antiquity.</note> as something true and historical, and believe that all the ornaments are false.

One must firmly fix this principle in one’s mind: that **Fables** are not entirely fictions; they are **Histories** of remote times <note>original: "tems reculés"</note> that have been disfigured—either by the ignorance of the common people, the artifice of Priests, or the genius of the **Poets**, who have always preferred the brilliant to the solid. But how is one to unravel all of this? One will often mistake fiction for the **truth**, and perhaps treat as a **Fable** the only circumstance that contains the truth. Are there rules for making a just discernment? Yes, without a doubt: one must first cast aside from a Fable everything that appears **supernatural**, all that pompous display of fictions that are so obvious to the eye. For example, from all the battles mentioned by **Homer**, first remove the **Gods** <note>original: "Dieux"</note> he involves in them; attribute to prudence and good conduct...

When Homer, for example, says (2) that <term>Aeolus</term> <note>The divine keeper of the winds in Greek mythology.</note> had given the winds to Odysseus enclosed in a skin, from which his companions let them escape, it is a veiled historical fact which teaches us that this Prince had predicted to Odysseus the wind that would blow for several days, and that he was only shipwrecked because he did not wish to follow his advice: but when Virgil adds (3) that the same Aeolus, at the request of Juno, stirred up a terrible storm that threw Aeneas’s fleet onto the coasts of Africa, it is a pure Fable based on the fact that Aeolus was regarded as the God of the Winds. Even the Fables we have called Philosophical were initially Historical, and it is only after the fact that the idea of natural things was attached to them: hence these mixed Fables,

# Mythology & Fables #

...so true, as I shall remark in the sequel, that the Pagans owed the existence of several of their Gods to some beautiful Statues or well-executed Paintings.

<margin>Sixth source. The plurality or the unity of names.</margin>
As it often happened that the same person bore several names—a practice very common among Oriental peoples—it was believed over the course of time, through the reading of poorly digested Histories and quite incompatible adventures, that different people were being discussed. Hence the multiplication of Heroes: the actions and travels of a single individual were divided among many. Mercury, for example, was called Thoth <note>original: "Thaut"; the Egyptian god of wisdom and writing</note> in Egypt, Teutates <note>original: "Teutat"; a Celtic deity</note> among our ancient Gauls, and Hermes among the Greeks. Pluto was known as Dis among the Celts, Hades <note>original: "Adès"</note> among the Greeks, Summanus <note>A Roman deity of nocturnal thunder</note> among the Latins, and Soranus <note>An Etruscan/Sabine god associated with the underworld and Mount Soracte</note> among the Sabines. And because a Hero or God was sometimes known in a particular country by only one name, with little knowledge of what he had done beyond those borders, when people encountered adventures other than those they had heard of, or different names and qualities, they did not doubt that they were dealing with different people; hence this prodigious number...

...of Jupiters, of Mercuries, etc. Sometimes the exact opposite was done; and when it happened that several people bore the same name, what should have been divided among many was instead attributed to only one. Thus, the history of the most famous figure was burdened with the adventures of all the others. Such is the history of the Hercules of Thebes, in which the actions and travels of the Phoenician Hercules and several other heroes of the same name were mixed together. Such also is the history of Jupiter, son of Saturn, in which the adventures of several Kings of Crete were gathered; they all bore the same name, which was common among these ancient kings, just as the name of Pharaoh or Ptolemy was in Egypt, or that of Caesar among the Roman Emperors.

Every River and every Fountain also had their **Tutelary Divinity** <note>A guardian spirit or god presiding over a specific place</note>; and whether rivers were given the names of the first Kings who had lived in the country where they flowed, or whether the Kings had taken their name from the rivers, as we shall discuss further below; they were later confused, and the Prince was deified in honor of the River. ### Expl. by History BOOK I. CHAP. IV. 8 ###

Thus were formed several **physical divinities** <note>Gods representing natural forces like wind or water</note>, and so many **astronomical fables** <note>Myths explaining the movements of stars and planets</note>, as we shall discuss in the following sections. This was a pitiful philosophy; but they had nothing better, and when the poets later came to embellish these **sensible ideas** <note>Concepts based on direct sensory perception rather than abstract scientific reasoning</note> with all the ornaments that their Muses—fertile in fiction—could provide, people took such pleasure in viewing nature only through these pleasant images that for quite a long time, they did not even think to push their discoveries any further.

The greatest harm was that **Religion** became entangled in this system: it multiplied its ceremonies with the invention of each new divinity, and those who wished to see a little more clearly were viewed as impious. Thus, the unfortunate **Anaxagoras** <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher (c. 500–428 BC) known for his materialist explanations of the universe</note> was punished with death <note>While the author states he was punished with death, historical sources often clarify that Anaxagoras was sentenced to death but instead went into exile with the help of Pericles</note> for having taught that the Sun was not a living being, and that it was merely a plate of steel the size of the **Peloponnese** <note>A large peninsula in southern Greece; Anaxagoras's point was that the sun was a physical object rather than a god</note>. One may conclude from everything we have just said that there is reason to believe that a portion of the **Ancient Philosophy** was contained within their fables, provided one is willing to admit that it was a very crude philosophy, and a system...

New ceremonies cost nothing to establish, and the reasons given for them were entirely fabulous <note>In this context, "fabulous" refers to "fables" or myths rather than historical facts.</note>. Stories forged by the Priests gave cause to change a sterile cult into another that might be more lucrative, and people were never too scrupulous on this point. As soon as some new Divinity was discovered, everyone vied to raise more Altars to them, and at the same time to proclaim more of their wonders.

# Mythology and Fables

And as a fellow-countryman God brought much prestige to his place of birth, everyone claimed his birth for their own: they fabricated records filled with fables; impostors supported alleged apparitions that the Priests had invented, and which the Poets then inserted into their works. From this comes that monstrous system, so full of fables, which <term>Pagan Theology</term> <note>The study of religious beliefs in non-Christian, polytheistic ancient societies, often viewed critically by 18th-century writers.</note> offers us.

<margin>Ninth source: The desire to have Gods for Ancestors.</margin>
Add to this that the most common mania of the great men of those times was the desire to descend from the Gods: to be a Hero, it was absolutely necessary to have Jupiter or Apollo as an ancestor; and since it was apparently not difficult then to find genealogists as accommodating as they are today, people had little trouble having titles drawn up where the ancestral root <note>original: "la souche"</note> was some God. Thus, almost all ancient genealogies were of this sort; the head of the line was Jupiter, after him came Hercules, etc.

<margin>Tenth source: Misunderstood Holy Scripture.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether Greek mythology is a corrupted version of biblical history, specifically examining the Phoenician author Sanchoniathon and the timeline of cultural exchange between the East and Greece.</meta>

### Explanation by History, Book I, Chapter V.

One cannot truly deny that Sanchoniathon <note>A legendary Phoenician author said to have lived before the Trojan War; his works are often cited in debates about the origins of religion.</note> alluded to the history of the first men, even though he completely distorted it, as I hope to show when we discuss the fragment of this author that Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a Christian historian who preserved fragments of earlier lost works.</note> has preserved for us. But did this writer—who lived before or shortly after the Trojan War, and who was known in Greece only through the translation by Philo of Byblos made in the time of Hadrian <note>Hadrian ruled as Roman Emperor from 117 to 138 AD.</note>—truly serve as the preceptor to Hesiod and Homer, in whose works the entire foundation of **Greek Mythology** is found? 

It is also true that the Greeks derived the knowledge of their gods from the Phoenicians and the Egyptians, through the colonies that arrived from those countries. However, the history of the Patriarchs <term>Patriarchs: the biblical fathers of the human race, such as Noah and his immediate descendants.</term> must have been quite obscured by the time of Inachus, Cecrops, and Cadmus <note>Legendary founders of Argos, Athens, and Thebes respectively, representing the earliest era of Greek civilization.</note>, as idolatry had already been widespread throughout the East for several centuries by then. 

Nevertheless, I will not fail to report the opinions of these scholars as the occasion arises, so that the reader—whom I seek to instruct in this work without wishing to compel them to follow one sentiment over another—may be in a position to judge for themselves which side they should take.

# Mythology and Fables

<margin>Eleventh source: Ignorance of ancient history.</margin>
<margin>(1) See the first Chapter.</margin>

A source more fertile and more favorable to the introduction of fables is the ignorance of ancient history and chronology. Since the use of letters <note>Meaning literacy and the use of an alphabet.</note> began only very late, especially in Greece, several centuries passed during which the memory of remarkable events was preserved only by tradition, or at most by a few monuments that later became quite ambiguous. Even when they began to use writing, they did not initially write continuous histories; they composed eulogies, hymns <term>Hymns: In this context, "cantiques," or sacred songs performed in honor of gods or heroes.</term>, and some genealogies filled with fables, which were prepared by the care of the priests, as has already been suggested (1). Consequently, one found nothing but confusion everywhere; and even when one wished to delve a little deeper into these ancient histories, after ascending through only three or four generations, one found oneself in the labyrinth of the history of the gods, where one always encountered Jupiter, Saturn, the Sky, and the Earth <note>In Greek mythology, these correspond to Zeus, Cronus, Uranus, and Gaia.</note>. The Greeks especially knew nothing more of their origins; that was where all their tradition ended, even among the most rational; for the others published...

# CHAPTER VI.
## Continuation of the same subject.

<margin>Thirteenth source. Ignorance of Languages.</margin>
Ignorance of languages, especially of **Phoenician**, has also been the source of an infinite number of **Fables** <note>In this context, "Fables" refers to the myths and legends of the ancient world.</note>. It is certain that the colonies departing from **Phoenicia** went to populate several regions of **Greece**; undoubtedly their language mixed with that of the countries where they settled (a): and as the **Phoenician language** has several ambiguous words, the **Greeks**—who later read their ancient history, which was filled with **Phoenician phrases**—having found these ambiguous words, did not fail to interpret them in the sense that most suited their taste. One should not even doubt that when they consulted the **Phoenicians**, who knew the penchant the Greeks had for fictions, the latter often deceived them. From this, an infinite number of **Fables** were born; here are several examples, taken mostly from **Bochart** <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667) was a French Protestant scholar who famously argued that Greek myths were often just misunderstood Phoenician words.</note>.

---

(a) **Bochart** and **Vossius** <note>Gerardus Vossius, a Dutch scholar of the 17th century, known for his work on classical history and theology.</note> have proven beyond rebuttal that the alphabet **Cadmus** <note>A legendary prince of Tyre who, according to Greek myth, founded the city of Thebes and brought the Phoenician alphabet to the Greeks.</note> brought to **Greece** was **Phoenician**; the alphabet previously used there was **Pelasgian** <note>A term for the indigenous, pre-Greek inhabitants of the Aegean region.</note>, and a language was formed from the fusion of the two.

Likewise, from the word *Sir*, which means a song or canticle, they created the Fable of the **Sirens**. **Aeolus** only passed among them for the God of winds and storms because the word *Eol*, or *Chol*, signifies a storm. The Greeks, who subsequently landed in the same place, not understanding the meaning of this word and remembering their own river Alpheus (2), imagined that since the fountain and the river had nearly the same name, they must have the same origin; and thereupon, some wit composed the Romance of the Loves of the River God with the Nymph Arethusa. Almost all subsequent Historians were then duped by this Fable and claimed that the Alpheus crossed the sea and emerged again on the Island of Sicily, near the fountain of Arethusa (*a*).

SANCHONIATHON, a Priest of Berytus <note>Ancient city in Phoenicia, modern-day Beirut, Lebanon.</note>, who lived—according to what is claimed—before the Trojan War, had written on the Cosmogony <note>The study of the origins of the universe.</note> and on the Theogony <note>The study of the origins and genealogy of the gods.</note> of the Phoenicians. # CHAPTER II.
## *Theogony of the Phoenicians.*

<margin>(1) Preparation for the Gospel, Book 1.</margin>
SANCHONIATHON, Priest of Berytus <note>Ancient Berytus is modern-day Beirut, Lebanon.</note>, who lived, it is claimed, before the Trojan War, had written on the Cosmogony <note>The origins of the universe.</note> and on the Theogony <note>The genealogy or origin of the gods.</note> of the Phoenicians. Eusebius, who has preserved for us a long fragment of this Treatise (1), reports in favor of this Author a passage that should not be considered suspicious, since it is taken from Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and famous critic of early Christianity; the author argues that because Porphyry was an "enemy," his praise of Sanchoniathon's accuracy regarding Jewish history is more credible.</note>, the greatest enemy that the Christians have ever had. This Author relates that Sanchoniathon had written about the Jews things that were *very true*; that he was in agreement with their *Writers*, and that he had learned several of the circumstances he reports from *Jerombaal, Priest of Jevo* <note>Jerombaal is often identified by scholars as Jerubbaal (Gideon) from the Bible, and Jevo is a Greek transcription of the Hebrew name for God, Yahweh.</note>; that he had dedicated his Work to *Abibalus, King of Phoenicia*; that not only this Prince, but those who were ordered to examine the books, had agreed upon the truth of this Author’s *History*.... Finally, that he had drawn what he put forward partly from the *Acts* <note>Official records or annals.</note> of individual cities, and partly from the *Archives* which were carefully preserved in the *Temples*.

# Mythology and Fables

[I]dolatry <note>The text begins mid-word from the previous page: "idolatry."</note> has made a point of speaking only of the descendants of Cain, who are rightly believed to have been the first authors of it. The second [point] is that he makes no mention of the Flood, which, according to the Church Fathers <note>The early influential theologians of the Christian Church.</note>, was the punishment for the crimes of that race, the greatest of which was the sacrilegious worship they had offered to created things. The third is that Sanchoniathon counts ten generations in the branch of Cain, whereas Moses lists only eight, passing from the third, or Enoch, to the sixth, or Irad. But it can be said that Moses, whose goal was to speak mainly of the race of Seth, or that of the Righteous, did not follow that of Cain in the same way, especially the fourth and fifth generations, perhaps because they were men who did not deserve to be named; for it is unlikely that the eight generations of Cain lasted as long as the ten of Seth mentioned by Moses. Finally, the fourth [point] is that the Phoenician author attributes most useful inventions to these descendants of Cain, just as Moses does, although these two authors are not always in agreement on the timing of these discoveries, nor on the persons who made them. ### Explanation by History, Book II, Chapter II

[Sanchonia]thon <note>The name is completed from the previous page: "Sanchoniathon," a semi-legendary Phoenician author.</note> attributing to one race what Moses attributes to another, as one can be convinced by reading the first chapters of Genesis.

I have said that these ten generations concerned the descendants of Cain, if one excepts Hypsistus <note>A name meaning "The Most High" in Greek</note>, because scholars—following Cumberland <note>Richard Cumberland (1631–1718), a Bishop who wrote a famous 18th-century analysis of Phoenician history</note>, who explained this fragment of the Phoenician author in great detail—claim that this Hypsistus was the father of Noah. They argue he is only mentioned in passing because he was an enemy of the idolaters, whose cause Sanchoniathon defends.

# Mythology & Fables

In the account of Moses, as we can see, the lineage of Cain ends with the last men I have just named, because they themselves, or their descendants, were swallowed up in the waters of the Deluge <note>The Great Flood of Noah</note>, without a single one being saved. How then, one might ask, was this lineage continued by Sanchoniathon in the third part of his excerpt which I am about to report? It is easy to answer this difficulty by saying that he took the figures of this second decade from the descendants of Noah. This will appear evident through the reflections that follow.

# CHAPTER III.

## *The Egyptian Theogony.*

**T**he Christian Apologists <note>Early Christian writers who defended their faith against critics and philosophers by comparing it to ancient religions.</note> were forced to search the deepest recesses of antiquity for the origins of other religions, and no one worked on this with more success than Eusebius of Caesarea <note>A 4th-century Greek historian and bishop, essential for preserving fragments of lost ancient works.</note>. How many precious fragments has he preserved for us, which the ravages of time would have destroyed, had it not been for the care he took to gather them in his work! Besides the famous fragment we discussed in the previous chapter, we owe him countless other pieces on the ancient religion of the Egyptians, the Greeks, and several other peoples. It is in his works that we see how idolatry grew, as well as the uncertainty and variations among philosophers regarding physical principles <note>In this context, the fundamental laws or natural elements that make up the universe.</note> and the origin of the world in particular. The fragment we have just related concerns, strictly speaking, only the Phoenicians; but who were the gods of Phoenicia, if not the gods of E— <note>The text continues as "Egypt" on the following page.</note>

### Explanation by History, Book II, Ch. III.

[in]telligence, the power it possessed to give life, its sovereignty over all things, and the spirituality of its movements. The egg coming out of its mouth designated the world, of which it was the artisan <note>or creator</note>. These same peoples also sometimes represented the Divinity under the symbol of a Serpent with the head of a Hawk, which, by opening its eyes, fills the world with light, and by closing them, covers it in darkness. One can confirm the opinion of the modern Author <note>Referring to Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688), whose work *The True Intellectual System of the Universe* is cited on the previous page.</note> by the testimony of Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote extensively on Egyptian mysteries and late-antique spirituality.</note>, who, during the time of Eusebius <note>The Bishop of Caesarea and historian (c. 260–339 AD).</note>, had applied himself greatly to studying the ancient Theology of the Egyptians, and who tried to prove—as Chaeremon <note>An Egyptian Stoic philosopher and librarian at Alexandria in the 1st century AD.</note> had previously asserted—that they did not generally believe that an inanimate nature was the origin of all things; but that in the world, as well as in ourselves, they recognized the soul as superior to nature, and the intelligence that created the world as superior to the soul.

Whatever ideas one attributes to the ancient Egyptian Philosophers, and to Thoth <note>original: "Thaut"; the Egyptian god of wisdom and writing, often identified by the Greeks as Hermes Trismegistus.</note> who was their Master, it is certain that their Theogony <note>The study of the origins and genealogy of the gods.</note> is a gross Idolatry, which was the origin and source of that of the Greeks and of several other nations, as will be seen in the following pages.

Such is, according to Diodorus of Sicily, the Cosmogony <note>A theory or story regarding the origin of the universe.</note> and the Theogony <note>A genealogy or account of the origin of the gods.</note> of the Egyptians; and it is easy to see that the Greeks had corrupted and adjusted it to their own manner. What one can conclude with the most certainty is that these ancient people recognized two sorts of Gods: the stars, especially the Sun and the Moon; and illustrious men, to whom they rendered religious worship because of the benefits they provided to humanity. But whether this theology was drawn from the Books of Thoth <note>original: "Thaut" or "Thot"; the Egyptian god of wisdom and writing.</note>, or from some tradition preserved by the Egyptian Priests, it is certain that the Greeks formed their own system from it, as will be seen in what follows.

# CHAPTER V.
## The Greek Theogony. <note>A "theogony" refers to an account of the origin and genealogy of a group of gods.</note>

<margin>
(1) Vol. II.
(1) Book 10.
</margin>
Greece never had anything but a very confused idea of the history of its religion. Devoted without reservation, on such an important subject, to its ancient *Poets*, it regarded them as its first *Theologians*; and yet these *Poets*, as *Strabo* (1) <note>Strabo (c. 64 BC–24 AD) was a Greek geographer and historian whose "Geography" is a vital source for ancient history.</note> judiciously remarks, whether through ignorance of antiquity or through flattery for the Greek princes, had adjusted all the *Genealogies* of their *Gods* in their favor, to make it believed that they were descended from them. Thus, when it is a question in their *Works* of one of their *Heroes*, one hardly needs to look back very far to find at the head of their *Genealogies* *Hercules*, *Jupiter*, or some other *God*. This foolish pretension of wanting to pass for being of great antiquity is remarkable in almost all *Peoples*; and the *Greeks* were the most stubborn in this regard. Thus we see with surprise that they, who could not have been unaware that they had received several *Colonies* <note>In this context, "colonies" refers to groups of settlers who brought their culture and religion from established civilizations to Greece.</note> from *Egypt* and *Phoenicia*,

### Mythology and Fables, Page 208

...to suppose a truly independent Being; most even agree on an eternity, an **Ontogony** <term>Ontogony [the study of the origin and generation of beings]</term>, or generation of Beings, some of whom are celestial, others terrestrial or infernal: but Demogorgon <note>original: "Daimogorgon"</note> and Achlys <note>Achlys represents the primordial mist or personified misery that existed before the world</note> exist in their system before the world, even before **Chaos**. Their Acmon and their Hypsistus exist before the Heavens, which the Romans call *Coelus* and the Greeks *Ouranos*. 

According to them, the Earth, Tartarus, and Love had preceded *Coelus*, since one finds in Hesiod that he is himself the son of the Earth. Phornutus, Hesychius, and Simmias of Rhodes, his Scholiast <note>an ancient commentator on a specific text</note>, regard Acmon as the father of *Coelus*; and this same Acmon is the son of Manes in the works of Polyhistor and Stephanus. 

*Coelus* was first the father of the **Hecatonchires** <term>Hecatonchires [the "Hundred-Handed" giants of Greek myth, known for their immense strength]</term>, then the Cyclopes, then the Titans, and of Saturn, who in his turn became the father of the other Gods. The Giants, children of the earth, came next, and Typhon is the last of all. After the Gods and the Giants—who are quite different, as one can see, from the Titans, who were Gods of the race of *Coelus*—came the demigods, born from the relations of Gods with mortal women, or of Goddesses with men.

In a word, the Greeks regarded as Gods those who had lived from the beginning of the world until the division they describe of the universe between Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto; that is to say, if one wishes to reconcile Fables with History, until the time of Peleg <note>original: "Phaleg"; a biblical figure whose name means "division," as the Earth was divided during his lifetime</note> and Nimrod <note>original: "Nemrod"; the biblical great-grandson of Noah, often associated with the construction of the Tower of Babel</note>. They knew the earliest times only very confusedly; a trait they shared with all peoples who have preserved ancient Annals, such as the Egyptians, the Chinese, etc. It is very easy to see that they have done nothing but alter the ancient Tradition, which Moses alone preserved, and that they have thereby fallen into the most monstrous errors. Here is a very authentic example, which will suffice for the present.

One finds in the text of the Septuagint <term>Septuagint [the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, which contains variations from the standard Masoretic text]</term> that the Giants emerged from the relations of Angels with the daughters of men. This opinion was even followed by the most ancient interpreters of Holy Scripture, as well as by Philo, Josephus, Saint Justin, Athenagoras, Clement of Alexandria, etc. Several learned Rabbis adopted it, and it is still generally received by all Muslims <note>original: "Mahometans"</note>. <margin>(1) *Dissertation on the Gods of Homer*. Memoirs of the Academy of Belles Lettres. Vol. 3, p. 1.</margin>

I would undoubtedly be blamed if, after having spoken in this chapter of **Orpheus**, **Hesiod**, and several other Greek poets, I said nothing of **Homer**, who, in his ***Iliad*** and ***Odyssey***, employed with such great display the same gods as Hesiod and Orpheus. However, it is worth noting that this great poet did not undertake, as the other two did, to provide a formal system for these same gods; he merely made use of the theology established in his own time. As **Abbé Fraguier** (1) <note>Claude-François Fraguier (1666–1728) was a French classical scholar and member of the Académie française, known for his work on ancient literature.</note> has judiciously observed, Homer is only a poet; if he is a theologian—as indeed he is, since he speaks of them at every turn and employs the ministry of the gods—he is so only by occasion, and not by way of a formal system. For what is a poet? He is a painter, an imitator; he does not produce his subject, but rather imitates and depicts it. Whatever ideas he may personally hold regarding his gods, since he speaks of them to please and to be understood, he never departs from the system accepted in his time.

### Mythology & Fables

From that point on, **Homer**, born in the heart of **Paganism** <note>The author uses "Paganism" in the traditional 18th-century sense to refer to the polytheistic religions of antiquity.</note>, could not have represented the Gods otherwise than he did. He did not invent the **Theology** he follows; he received it. But as time, which destroys errors, has respected his works, and since this great Poet knew how to utilize everything that a false Religion provided him, it was believed later on that he was the father and inventor of so many extraordinary and bizarre things, of which, in fact, he was only the Copyist and the Painter.

**Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman statesman and philosopher.</note> complains that Homer lowered the Gods to the level of men, instead of elevating men to the perfection of the Gods. This reproach is unjust. Most of Homer's Gods had been men who, through brilliant actions and the invention of the Arts, had earned divine honors. However, these actions, however brilliant they might be, were not always according to the rules of strict integrity. Morality did not always possess the purity to which **Pythagoras** and **Plato** <note>Pythagoras (6th century BCE) and Plato (4th century BCE) are credited here with introducing more refined, abstract, and ethically rigorous standards to Greek thought.</note> later restricted it. Strength, talents, and the gifts of nature long took the place of true merit; and because it was these qualities that had consecrated <note>Meaning their deification or transformation into "sacred" figures.</note> these great men, such things were believed worthy of them even after their deification.

### Explanation by History, Book II, Chapter V

215

In a word, deified men possessed both divine perfection and human weakness; thus the Poet was obliged to represent them according to these two ideas. Consequently, one must see in them a mixture of grandeur and smallness, of strength and weakness, of majesty and debasement, of brilliant virtues and shameful vices.

It is clear from what I have just said that the Greeks possessed several **Theogonies** <note>Accounts or poems describing the origins and genealogies of the gods.</note>, and that they had reduced to a system the **Theology** they had received from the peoples of the **Orient** <note>Specifically referring to the ancient Near East, such as Egypt and Phoenicia, from which many Greek myths were thought to have originated.</note>. The **Romans** had nothing similar. Content with the Religion of the Greeks and the other Peoples they had conquered, they took their Divinities, worship, ceremonies, sacrifices, Priests, and festivals; in a word, all the apparatus that **Idolatry** <note>The worship of idols or multiple deities; used here to describe the complex visual and ritual nature of Roman religion.</note> brought with it, without ever having thought of reducing such a motley Religion to a system. Thus, the most idolatrous city in the world was the one that most neglected the history of its gods. **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman statesman and philosopher.</note>, to be sure, provides some genealogies in his *Treatise on the Nature of the Gods* <note>original: "De Natura Deorum"</note>: but as he most often uses ideas he had drawn from the books of the Greeks, and as he disputes this matter as an **Academician** <note>A follower of the Academic school of philosophy, which practiced skepticism and preferred to weigh various arguments rather than state a single, dogmatic truth.</note>, one cannot

### Explained by History, Book I, Chapter VII.

Fo <note>The Chinese name for the Buddha.</note> and his cult were introduced there.

Such was the dominant religion of China in the early times of their Empire: I say the dominant religion because the people did not cease to acknowledge subaltern spirits <note>Lesser deities or spiritual beings subordinate to a supreme power, similar to local saints or guardian spirits.</note> who watched over the cities and the countryside, and they honored them with a superstitious cult to ask them for health, success in business, and abundant harvests. Mixed into this cult were several superstitious practices that bordered on Magic, to which these people have always been quite addicted; but this was not the religion of the state. The Tribunal of Rites <note>The *Li-pu*, the imperial ministry responsible for state ceremonies and religious orthodoxy.</note> always condemned these kinds of practices, even though several of the Mandarins <note>High-ranking scholar-officials of the Chinese imperial administration.</note> who composed it often had a taste for them themselves.

Thus, to speak accurately, the Chinese do not have what we call Theogony <note>An account of the origin and genealogy of the gods.</note> or Cosmogony <note>A theory or story concerning the origin and evolution of the universe.</note>. Their philosophers, solely attached to morality, politics, and history, always neglected Physics <note>In this historical context, "physics" refers to "natural philosophy," the study of the laws of nature and the physical world.</note>; and one does not find in their writings—I am speaking of the ancient ones—those systems so well known in Europe, Egypt, and in some parts of Asia, regarding the formation of the world and the bodies that compose it.

## CHAPTER X.

### *Of Pagan Theology, and particularly that of the Poets.*

After having presented the various **Theogonies** <term>Accounts of the origins and genealogies of the gods.</term> of the Ancients, that is to say, the theologies specific to each nation, it will not be useless to make known more specifically the general theology of Paganism, especially that of the Greeks and their poets. My design is not to detail all its horrors; such a task would be useless today. The first **Fathers of the Church** <note>Early Christian theologians and writers who established the intellectual and doctrinal foundations of Christianity.</note> and the **Apologists** <term>Early Christian writers who defended their faith against legal attacks and pagan philosophy.</term> of the Christian religion, who found themselves obliged to do so—since it was necessary to sap the foundations of Paganism, which was the dominant religion of their time—had to do it, and they acquitted themselves with such erudition and such force that they finally obliged the most enlightened philosophers to explain, through often ingenious allegories, a system whose mere description inspired horror. This is what they were reduced to by Saint Justin, Arnobius, Athenagoras, and Lactan- <note>Continuing on the next page: "Lactantius." These were prominent early Christian authors who wrote extensively against Roman and Greek polytheism.</note>

Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC) was an ancient Roman scholar and writer known as "the most learned of the Romans."</note> distinguished three kinds of Theology: the Mythical <term>μυθικὴ (mythikē): relating to fables and stories</term>, the Physical <term>φυσικὴ (physikē): relating to the natural world</term>, and the Political <term>πολιτικὴ (politikē): relating to the state or city-state</term>, which St. Augustine translates with these words: *mythical, natural or philosophical, and civil* <note>original: "fabularis, naturalis, vel philosophica, civilis."</note>. The first was the Theology of the Poets; the second, that of the Philosophers; and the third, that of the Ministers of Religion. Varro tried to make use of this distinction, of which Quintus Scaevola, the sovereign Pontiff <note>The *Pontifex Maximus*, the highest-ranking priest in Roman state religion.</note>, is believed to be the author—the very same who was killed by one of those murderers employed by Marius <note>Quintus Mucius Scaevola was murdered in 82 BC during the Roman civil wars between the factions of Marius and Sulla.</note>.

<margin>(1) Of the City of God.</margin>
The Theology of the Poets was rejected by the sages of Paganism. Varro, as St. Augustine reports (1), confessed that it attributed to the Gods actions that one would be ashamed to attribute to the lowest of men: *Finally, in this [theology] all things are attributed to the Gods—* <note>original Latin: "Denique, in hac omnia Diis attri-". This is a critique of the scandalous behavior of gods in classical myths, such as theft and adultery.</note>

I mean the **Trojan War**. This war caused the death of an infinite number of people and ruined a beautiful Kingdom; it was followed by countless miseries, storms, fires, and everything that accompanies great desolation. All the **Gods** took sides; **Olympus** <note>The mountain home of the Greek gods, here representing the divine assembly.</note> found itself divided into two factions. There were no intrigues, schemes, or clever tricks that each of the **Gods** did not employ; one certainly cannot accuse them of negligence during this entire war; their **Providence** <term>Providence: The protective care of God or of nature as a spiritual power.</term> did not lack for employment. **Homer** describes all their movements with infinite detail; the other **Poets** have followed his example. This is, therefore, a very suitable vantage point to convince ourselves of their **Theological** sentiment regarding providence: let us see then what the motive for this war was; let us go back to the source.

Was it a matter of punishing an impious nation, of avenging the oppressed innocent, or the **Gods** themselves being despised; or of giving the universe a signal example of justice and equity? Anything but that: it was a matter of avenging a **Goddess** for the contempt shown toward her beauty. <note>The author refers to the "Judgment of Paris," where the Trojan prince Paris was asked to judge who was the most beautiful among Juno, Minerva, and Venus. [...developed], it is only to make them scoundrels. You will not see these Gods eager to punish impiety or injustice; they only vent their rage on those who forget them during some sacrifice, or who compare their hair or their complexion to that of some Goddess: similar to those petty provincial Lords, who care very little whether their vassals are scoundrels and libertines <note>In this context, "libertines" refers to those living without moral or religious restraint, a common 18th-century term for social and moral deviants.</note>, provided they do not hunt on their lands, and that they occasionally give presents to their wives.
