This would be the place to explain the <term>Theology of the Poets</term> <note>This refers to "mythical theology," or the religious ideas found in the works of poets like Homer and Ovid, which the author contrasts with "natural" or "rational" theology.</note> concerning the morals of their Gods: but I would fear making the Reader blush at the account of the infamies they relate. # Explanation through History, Book II, Ch. I

everyone will agree with him; but he chose not to notice that the word <term>eidos</term> <note>original Greek: εἶδος; refers to the "form" or "essence" of a thing.</note> signifies the essential, internal, and true form of a thing, and that the word "idol" designates the external form, or the representation of that same thing, whether large or small. In short, the real form and physical extent of the human body, consisting of the assembly of its flesh, bones, and skin, is called <term>eidos</term>; but the representation of this same body, whether painted or sculpted in relief, was called <term>eidolon</term> <note>original Greek: εἴδωλον</note>, meaning a **"little form,"** a false and merely apparent form.

There are scholars who derive the etymology of the name "Idol" from two Greek words, one of which means **"image"** and the other **"pain,"** following the Hebrew word <term>Hatsabbim</term> <note>original: הָעֲצַבִּים (hatzabbim). In the Hebrew Bible, this term for idols is derived from a root meaning "to fashion" but is homonymous with the word for "pains" or "sorrows," a connection often exploited by theologians to suggest that false gods bring only misery.</note>, which means the same thing. This is to convey that Idols are the source of pain and, at the same time, of the punishments with which God penalized those who abandoned themselves to their worship.

This being established, by the word **idolatry**, one should understand the worship rendered to statues and other representations of the Gods, and by the word **Idols**, everything that represented them.

### Explanation by History, Book III, Chapter III

> "...[to have] neither temples, nor idols, there being at that time neither painting, nor the art of pottery, nor even sculpture, nor masonry or architecture—I believe that every thinking person perceives this very clearly. But beyond all that, people did not even speak of those Gods and Heroes so renowned since then; there was at that time no Jupiter, nor Saturn, nor Neptune, nor Juno, nor Minerva, nor Bacchus, nor any other male or female God, such as were found by the thousands in later times among both the Greeks and the Barbarians <note>In this context, "Barbarians" refers to any non-Greek civilizations, such as the Egyptians or Persians.</note>. # Explanation by History, Book III, Chapter III

the Guebres <term>Guebres: A historical term, often used by Europeans and Muslims, to refer to the Zoroastrian population of Persia who continued to practice the ancient religion of the Magi.</term>, who inhabit the southern extremities of Persia, near the borders of the Mughal <note>original: "Mogol"; refers to the Mughal Empire in the Indian subcontinent.</note> Empire.

There are scholars who believe that the ancient philosophers, especially those of Chaldea <note>An ancient region in southern Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq) renowned for its early advancements in astronomy and astrology.</note>, gave rise to Sabianism. It is true, indeed, that they reasoned much about the stars, their influences, and their beauty; perhaps they even believed that they were eternal beings, and thus so many deities, or at least that there were Gods who inhabited them and regulated their course and influences. They even claimed—and this opinion is very ancient—that the body of the star was merely its carriage, or a kind of skiff <note>A small boat; the author refers to the ancient belief that celestial bodies were vessels carrying divine beings across the sky.</note>, which served to carry the Gods who guided them.

But was so much reasoning required for carnal and unrefined men to be compelled to address their first prayers to these brilliant and luminous bodies? Was it not enough for them to turn their eyes toward the Sun, to see how, beyond the way it illuminates the world, it provides it with heat and fertility, to judge that it was like the father of nature, that it gave it life, and that without it, nature would be but an expanse without life, without light, and without—

Did all the peoples who have worshipped the Sun—the Mexicans <note>The indigenous peoples of the Aztec Empire and surrounding regions.</note>, the Peruvians <note>The indigenous peoples of the Inca Empire.</note>, and the other savages of the New World—wait for the decisions of philosophers before addressing their vows and prayers to this luminous star? Be that as it may, Sabianism <term>Sabianism: An ancient religious system centered on the worship of the stars and celestial bodies.</term> must be regarded as the most ancient sect of the pagan world. It began shortly after the Deluge <note>The Great Flood of Noah.</note>, as it was known to the ancestors of Abraham—to Terah <note>original: "Tharé"; the father of the biblical patriarch Abraham.</note> and Serug <note>original: "Sarug"; the great-grandfather of Abraham.</note>—and perhaps even before them. It is the sect that has made the most progress; I have spoken of the various peoples who had adopted it, and if the most learned Rabbis and Oriental authors are to be believed, it infected almost the entire world. Finally, of all the sects, it is the one that has lasted the longest, since there are still a great many idolaters who follow it.

# CHAPTER IV.
## *On the Progress of Idolatry.*

The first humans, some time after their dispersal, were extremely unrefined; and the Greeks, who later became so civilized, were initially no less so than those they grew accustomed to calling Barbarians, if we are to believe Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BC, known for his monumental universal history, the *Bibliotheca historica*.</note>. Thus, one must not imagine that in the beginning Idolatry was a reasoned system, or that Theology was then burdened with that array of ceremonies that were added to it later. Nothing was simpler, nor at the same time cruder, than the Religion of the first Idolaters. Scarcely any expense was made, either to represent the Gods or to pay them religious worship. Pausanias <note>A Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century AD whose descriptions of ancient Greece provide vital links between myth and geography.</note> informs us that the Athenians, in the time of Cecrops <note>The legendary first king and founder of Athens, said to have introduced the first elements of civilization.</note>, offered only simple cakes to the celestial Jupiter <note>The Roman name used here for the Greek god Zeus.</note>; and as they called these cakes *Bous* <note>original: "Bous"; a Greek term for "ox".</note>, it has been incorrectly believed that they sacrificed oxen to him. The Scythians <note>An ancient nomadic people of Central Eurasia known for their warlike culture.</note>, according to Saint Clement of Alexandria (1), worshiped <note>(1) *Exhortation to the Greeks* (original: "Orat. ad Gent."); a work by the Christian theologian Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215 AD) criticizing pagan practices.</note>

<summary>This page argues that early idolatry was not a complex theological system, but rather a simple and crude practice born from unrefined ancient cultures. It cites historical examples, such as the Athenians offering simple cakes rather than expensive animal sacrifices to their gods.</summary>
<keywords>origins of idolatry, Greek history, Diodorus Siculus, Cecrops, Zeus, animal sacrifice, Saint Clement of Alexandria, Scythians</keywords>

What began to give great momentum to idolatry, and what must therefore be placed among the primary causes of its progress, was the invention of the Arts, especially painting and Sculpture. Well-crafted Statues attract more respect, and people had less difficulty believing that the Gods they represented actually inhabited them. Often, Statues even increased the number of Gods; as *St. Augustine* <note>A 4th-century Christian theologian and philosopher whose writings often analyzed the origins of pagan beliefs</note> remarks regarding the *Muses*, who were originally only three, as will be related in their history: but having been represented by three different Sculptors, their statues appeared so beautiful that all nine were consecrated; and they augmen-

### *Of the Temples of the Pagans, of their Form, of their Antiquity, &c.*

The antiquity of <term>Temples: Buildings dedicated to the worship of a deity or deities.</term> is as undeniable as the time at which people first began to build them is uncertain. Although men and women generally entered the **Temples**, there were some where entry was forbidden to men, such as that of **Diana** in Rome, on the street named *Vicus Patricius* <note>Latin: "The Street of the Patricians," an ancient residential street on the Viminal Hill</note>, as **Plutarch** <note>A Greek biographer and philosopher who wrote extensively on Roman customs</note> informs us, even though they could enter other Temples of this Goddess; it is believed that the reason for this prohibition was that a woman who was praying in this Temple had received the most grievous insult there. ### *Temple of Belus.*

<margin>(1) Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 1, Ch. 10.</margin>
If this Temple was the oldest of all those of Paganism <note>The author uses "Paganism" to refer broadly to the polytheistic religions of the ancient world</note>, as one cannot doubt, it was also the most singular for its structure. Berosus <note>A Babylonian priest and historian from the 3rd century BCE</note>, as reported by Josephus (1), attributes its construction to Belus, who was himself worshipped there after his death. But it is certain that if the Belus mentioned by this historian is the same as Nimrod <note>A biblical figure and king of Shinar, traditionally credited with commissioning the Tower of Babel</note>, as is very likely, his intention was not to build a Temple, but to raise a tower that could protect him and his people from floods, should any occur similar to the Deluge. We know in what manner God halted this foolish design. The work remained in the state it was in at the moment of the confusion of languages, and was destined in the following years to serve as a Temple to Belus, who after his death merited divine honors. ### Temple of Vulcan at Memphis.

The Egyptians, according to Herodotus, were the first of all Peoples to construct Temples in honor of the Gods. I do not intend to speak of all those that were in that country; but that of Vulcan <note>The author uses "Vulcan" to refer to the Egyptian creator-god Ptah, following the common practice of Greek and Roman writers who identified foreign deities with their own</note> and several others deserve, because of their antiquity, for us to go into some detail regarding them.

Chersiphron had even more difficulty placing a stone of much greater weight above the temple door: one might think that Pliny, for lack of a factual account, had imagined the manner in which they succeeded in placing this enormous mass; but instead, he coldly reports a vision of the architect to whom Diana appeared, exhorting him to take courage, and says that the next morning the stone was seen to descend by itself and place itself where it was meant to be: *And thus the next day the stone appeared, and seemed to have been settled by its very weight.* <note>original: "Atque ita poſtridiè apparuit lapis, pondereque ipſo correctus videbatur." quoted from Pliny the Elder’s *Natural History*</note> One might well believe that the roof of the temple was made of cedar planks, as the same author says; but I do not know if one should give credit to what he says of the staircase by which one climbed to the roof, which was made of a single grapevine. ### Temple of Olympian Jupiter.

Greece possessed such a great number of Temples, Chapels, and Altars that one encountered them at every step in the cities, in the small towns, and in the countryside. To be convinced of this, one only has to read the Ancients, and especially Pausanias <note>Pausanias was a 2nd-century AD Greek traveler and geographer whose writings provide a detailed eyewitness account of ancient Greek monuments.</note>, who was particularly dedicated to describing them and who speaks of them on almost every page of his travels through Greece.

Among so many Temples, Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio was a Roman architect and engineer whose multi-volume work 'On Architecture' became the foundational text for Western classical building.</note> especially admired four, which were built of marble and enriched with such beautiful ornaments that they were the admiration of the most skillful connoisseurs; they became the rule and the model for buildings in the three orders of Architecture: the Doric, the Ionic, and the Corinthian. The first of these beautiful works was the Temple of Diana at Ephesus, the description of which we have just seen. ### The Pantheon of Rome.

Rome and Italy possessed no fewer Temples than Greece. They were to be found everywhere, and several were remarkable, either for their singularity or for their magnificence. One must place among the most beautiful that of **Jupiter**, upon the **Capitoline Hill** <note>The Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, the most important temple in Ancient Rome.</note>, and that of Peace, which, according to **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist of the 1st century CE.</note>, were two of the finest ornaments of Rome. # CHAPTER VII.
## On Sacred Groves.

In addition to Temples, Chapels, <term>Lararia</term> <note>Private shrines located within a Roman home, dedicated to the Lares, or household guardian spirits.</note>, and Altars, Paganism had yet other places destined for the worship of the Gods. These were the **Sacred Groves**, the establishment of which is so ancient that it is believed to even precede that of Temples and Altars. ...that high point of perfection where it <note>Referring to the art of sculpture.</note> became admired, especially in **Greece**, for the masterpieces it produced. From this, one must suppose that the first **Statues of the Gods**, although guided by this new art, were still very crude. Neither the legs nor the arms were separated, but were joined to the rest of the material that had been used to form the figure. They had closed eyes, and at most the arms were hanging and as if glued along the body, with the feet joined; nothing was animated, there was no posture, no gesture. For the most part, they were square and shapeless figures that ended in a sheath <note>Original: *gaîne*; this refers to the pillar-like base of a "herm," where the lower body is a block rather than carved legs.</note>. ### Explanation through History: Book III, Chapter IX.

...by means of design and solid material, [sculpture] imitates nature. Its materials include wood, stone, marble, ivory, and different metals, such as gold, silver, and copper, as well as precious stones, and so on. It also encompasses casting, which is subdivided into the art of making figures in wax and that of casting all sorts of metals in foundries. **Statuaries** <note>A historical term for sculptors, specifically those who crafted statues of the gods or notable figures.</note> were free to use all these materials and all these forms for the statues of the Gods. History teaches us that there were statues of all these kinds; they were made from the most precious woods and those least subject to decay.

The statue of **Jupiter** at **Sicyon** <note>A powerful city-state in the Peloponnese, known as a center of ancient Greek art.</note> was made of boxwood; and at **Ephesus**, that of **Diana** was made of cedar. If one has the curiosity to find statues of Gods of all the forms and all the materials of which I have spoken, one has only to read **Pausanias** <note>Pausanias (c. 110 – 180 AD) was a Greek traveler and geographer whose "Description of Greece" is a crucial source for ancient art and architecture.</note>, who describes them of every kind.

Generally speaking, the statues of the Gods, after the invention of Sculpture, were only of molded earth, and as fragile as simple vessels. This art of casting earth or clay in a mold is called **earthenware** <note>original: *fictilis*</note>, and the works that come from it, **pottery** <note>original: *fictilia*</note>. Holy Scripture, and the Prophets above all, constantly reproach the Pagans for adoring these sorts of idols. Later, these statues were laden with different colors, and finally, they were gilded. The Romans, whose religion reflected the simplicity of their customs for a long time, only began very late to have these gilded statues; theirs, until then, had only the color of the earth from which they were made. **Pliny** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (AD 23–79), a Roman author and natural philosopher who wrote the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note> praises this early Roman simplicity. *Men,* he says, *who sincerely honored such Gods, should not make us ashamed.* <note>original Latin: "Hæ tùm effigies Deorum erant laudatiſſimæ, nec pœnitet nos illo-" [rum]. Translation: "These were then the most highly praised images of the Gods, nor are we ashamed of those [who worshipped them]."</note>

# Explanation by History Book III. Ch. IX. 441

in them that people placed all their confidence. Vows were made to them, sacrifices were offered to them, and prayers were addressed to them; it was from them that health and other blessings were expected, as well as deliverance from evils and public calamities. This respect and this confidence were based not only on the fact that they represented the Gods, but because people also believed that the Gods themselves inhabited the statues and listened to vows and prayers from within them.

On the day of the Feasts of each of these Gods, care was taken to adorn their Statues with everything that seemed likely to embellish them; ribbons, small bandages <note>Often referred to as fillets or *vittae*, these were ceremonial headbands or ribbons used to decorate sacred objects.</note>, and branches; everything was employed. They were anointed with oil, or rubbed with wax to make them more lustrous; and this custom was especially practiced regarding the **Lares** and the **Penates** <note>Roman household deities who protected the home and the family's food stores.</note>. 

Although the manner of representing the Gods was not uniform, there were nevertheless customs that were quite generally observed. Thus, **Jupiter** was given a noble and majestic air, which announced the Master of the world, and he usually appears with a beard. **Apollo**, who is depicted as a young man, wears none; **Bacchus** sometimes has one, and then he is called the **Bearded** <note>original: "Barbatus". ### Explanation by History, Book III, Chapter IX.

-priate to several Gods, those Statues that bear them are called *Pantheistic* <note>original: *Pan-thées*. These statues combined the attributes of multiple deities into a single figure.</note>, such as those of *Harpocrates* <note>The Greek god of silence, adapted from the Egyptian child-god Horus.</note> and several others usually are. Egyptian Statues were more heavily laden with these symbols than those of the Greeks and the Romans, as can be seen in the works of Antiquaries <note>Historians or collectors of ancient artifacts.</note>. These symbols were taken from trees, plants, or animals, which for particular reasons were dear to the Gods, as we shall discuss when speaking of Sacrifices, Offerings, and Victims, which were usually chosen from among the things believed to be pleasing to them.

The reasons for this predilection of the Gods were sometimes mysterious, and the Ancients did not dare to report them; often, however, they are known. Thus, to give only a few examples, the laurel was dear to *Apollo* because of *Daphne*; the pine to *Cybele* because of *Atys*; and the poplar to *Hercules*, because he had brought one from the land of the *Hyperboreans* <note>A legendary people who lived in a land of perpetual sunshine in the far north.</note>, etc.

Almost always, the Statues of the Gods were simple and presented only a single figure; sometimes they were grouped and contained several.

# CHAPTER X.

## Concerning Sacrifices and Victims.

Sacrifice is an act of Religion by which man acknowledges the Divinity of the one to whom he offers it, intending to honor them in the most authentic manner, to thank them for the blessings he believes he has received, and to ask for new ones. In the earliest times of Paganism, the worship rendered to the Gods was very simple: the Egyptians, if we are to believe Theophrastus, cited by Porphyry (1), anciently offered to 
<margin>(1) Book on Abstinence <note>original: *Lib. de Abst.* (De Abstinentia)</note> in Eusebius’s *Preparation for the Gospel* <note>original: *Præp. Ev.* (Praeparatio Evangelica)</note> Book I. ch. 9.</margin>
their Gods not incense and perfumes, but green herbs that they gathered by hand, which they presented to them as the first productions of nature. Ovid depicts the simplicity of these first Sacrifices very well: *Incense*, he says, *had not yet come from the banks of the Euphrates, nor costus <term>costus: an aromatic plant root from India used in ancient perfumes</term> from the far reaches of India. Saffron was not yet known, and they were content to place grass or laurel upon the altar.*

Among the **Athenians**, the *Victim-slayer* <term>original: *Victimaire*; the sacrificial assistant who struck the animal with an axe or knife</term>, after having struck the animal intended for sacrifice, was forced to flee with all his might. He was pursued, and to avoid being caught, he would throw away the axe he had used, as if it alone were guilty of the death of the animal being sacrificed. Those who followed him would seize this axe and bring a lawsuit against it. Whoever took up its defense would argue that the axe was less guilty than the *Grinder* <term>original: *Remouleur*; the craftsman who sharpened the blades</term> who had sharpened it; the *Grinder*, when accused, would shift the blame onto the stone used for sharpening, and so on, so that the trial never ended. This was a ridiculous ceremony, in truth, but it proved the aversion the **Athenians** had for **bloody sacrifices**.

But it is worth noting that even at the time when living victims were sacrificed, the ancient form of sacrifice—consisting only of herbs, salt, and flour—had not been forgotten, and it was still used as the most fitting way to appease the Gods; this is what led **Horace** <note>A famous Roman lyric poet (65–8 BCE) known for his Odes and Satires</note> to say:

Afterward, the victim was cut into pieces, which were then cooked and distributed for the feast. In the burnt offering, it was entirely consumed by fire, so that nothing of it remained. Sometimes only the blood was sprinkled around the altar; the fat surrounding the internal organs <note>original: "viſceres".</note> was burned upon it, and the rest was taken away or eaten near the very place of the ritual slaughter <note>original: "immolation".</note>. All those present were obliged to keep silence while the victim was being slaughtered and while it burned upon the Altar. In the interval between these two operations, they were permitted to speak with one another; from this came the proverb, *between the slaughter and the offering* <note>original Latin: "inter cæsa & porrecta"; this phrase was used to describe a moment of leisure or a delay between two important actions</note>.

When the Priest went to sacrifice, a Herald cried out before him, *do this* <note>original Latin: "hoc age"</note>, meaning: be solely attentive to what you are about to do. And in Greece, when he approached the Altar, he would ask: *Who is here?* and the Assistants would respond: *Many good people.* Then the Priest pronounced the formula, *Begone, all you wicked ones*, which the Romans rendered with these words, *stay far away, you profane ones* <note>original Latin: "procul este profani"</note>. The Priests who performed the sacrifice usually had their heads veiled; I say usually, because there were Sacrifices where they were required to be bareheaded. There is not much agreement on this distinction: however, Fabretti (1) <note>Raffaele Fabretti (1618–1700) was a noted Italian antiquarian and authority on Roman inscriptions.</note> believes that the head was veiled when sacrificing to the twelve great Gods <term>Twelve Great Gods: The *Dii Consentes*, the primary pantheon of Rome which included Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, etc.</term>, and that one sacrificed to the others with the head uncovered. Plutarch <note>A Greek philosopher and historian who wrote extensively on Roman customs.</note> seems to insinuate that the Priest only covered his head when sacrificing to the celestial Gods, since he says that the one who offered the Sacrifice to Saturn had his head bare, because he was one of the infernal Gods <note>Though Saturn was a major deity, he was sometimes associated with the underworld or ancient, "earth-bound" rites.</note>. We only know that in Greece, the Sacrificer was always bareheaded.

<margin>(3) Aeneid, Book 2.</margin>

But it is worth noting that this ablution <term>Ablution: A ritual washing or cleansing of the body or objects.</term> was only required for Sacrifices offered to the celestial Gods; sprinkling <note>original: *l’aspersion*</note> being sufficient for the terrestrial and infernal Gods. In Rome, one never performed a sacrifice without first addressing a prayer to Janus, for the reason—says Ovid <note>A famous Roman poet known for his works on mythology and customs.</note>—that he was the guardian of the gate that led to the other Gods. Once this prayer was finished, a second was made to Jupiter, then a third to Juno; or according to others, to Vesta. The Priest then circled the Altar several times and brought his hand to his mouth <note>A ritual gesture of reverence or a call for silence.</note>; then he poured wine onto the same Altar with the *patera* <term>Patera: A shallow, broad bowl used to pour liquid offerings during a sacrifice.</term>: finally, he ordered the Victim-maker <term>Victim-maker: A translation of "Victimaire" (Victimarius), an assistant tasked with the physical killing of the sacrificial animal.</term> to strike the victim; this he did either with the knife called the *secespita* <term>Secespita: A long iron knife with a round handle used by Roman priests.</term>, or by knocking it unconscious with a blow from a mallet.

The Taurobolium <term>Taurobolium: A ritual sacrifice of a bull, often associated with the worship of the goddess Cybele, where the initiate was "cleansed" by the blood of the animal.</term> was a Sacrifice offered to the mother of the Gods <note>original: "mere des Dieux"; referring to the goddess Cybele, the Phrygian Earth-Mother.</note>. Let us finish this Chapter with some general observations regarding the formulas of prayers used there. As it was believed that the Gods themselves had dictated these formulas, they were regarded as something so essential that if the person charged with reciting them forgot or transposed even a single word, it was believed that the Sacrifice became useless. Thus, when the **Consul Decius** devoted himself to the infernal Gods <note>The *devotio* was a Roman ritual where a general sacrificed his life to the gods of the underworld in exchange for victory</note>, and the enemy troops with him, he warned the **Pontiff Valerius Maximus** <note>original: "Valere Maxime"</note> to pronounce exactly the formula prescribed for this occasion. There were even men appointed to ensure that nothing of the Liturgy <note>original: "Formulaire"</note> was forgotten; and so that they could hear the one reciting it without losing a single word, they imposed silence on those attending. ## CHAPTER XI.

### *On the Instruments used in Sacrifices and other religious Ceremonies.*

After having treated Sacrifices and victims, I must speak of the sacred instruments: but as it is difficult to make their description well understood without figures, readers will have recourse to the Antiquarians <note>Historical scholars who studied and cataloged the physical remains and artifacts of the ancient world</note> who have had them engraved.

The one named the ***Acerra*** <note>original: "Acerra," a Latin term for an incense box</note> was a small casket in which incense was placed, much like those we have in our churches; for those of the Ancients, which time has preserved for us, and which...

The **Patera** was an instrument that was ordinarily round, slightly hollowed, and with a handle. It served to receive the liquid poured from the vase and to spread it upon the victim; something which **Virgil** explains very clearly.

Since the vapor <note>original: "exhalaiſon"; the natural gas or fumes believed to induce a prophetic trance</note> that inspired her with the future issued from a cavern, as we shall say in the *History of the Oracles*, and since one could fall into it by approaching too closely—which had happened sometimes—they invented a machine supported by three feet which rested upon the rock, and the **Priestess** sat upon it to receive the vapor from the cavern conveniently and without danger. The second species includes everything that was supported on three feet: vases, tables, or whatever else it might be; and of these, there were a great number. I place in the third species the votive **Tripods**, which **Princes** or **Private Individuals** consecrated in the **Temples of Apollo**. **Herodotus** (1) <note>Herodotus, the 5th-century BCE Greek historian known as the "Father of History"; the citation refers to Book IX of his *Histories*</note> speaks of a golden **Tripod** that the **Greeks**, victorious over the **Persians**, sent to **Delphi**: *In the division they made of the enemy's spoils*, says this Author, *they set the silver aside, took a tenth of it for the God honored at Delphi; and they made from this portion a golden Tripod which they consecrated to him, and which is still seen upon...*

...is now necessary to say something of the Priests and the Ministers. As there is no nation, however savage it may be, that does not have some Religion, there is likewise none that does not have Ministers to preside over it: but in this Chapter, we shall hardly speak of any but those of the **Greeks** and the **Romans**. To do so successfully, we shall take as our guide the illustrious **Mr. Potter, Bishop of Oxford**, who wrote an excellent work on *Greek Archaeology* <note>Referring to *Archaeologia Graeca* by John Potter (1674–1747), a standard reference on Greek antiquities for over a century.</note>.

### *Priests of the Greeks.*

The **Greeks**, the most polished of all idolatrous nations, and almost the only one not qualified by the name of Barbarian; this Nation, I say, had its Priests, its worship, and its Sacrifices. But as all of **Greece** was divided into several different states, each of these Peoples had its own rites and ceremonies of Religion: all had their Priests, whose general name was <term>priest</term> <note>original Greek: *ἱερεὺς* (hiereus)</note>: but from the time of **Homer**, one finds the name of <term>one who prays</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀρητὴρ* (arētēr)</note> given to **Chryses** <note>In the *Iliad*, Chryses is the priest of Apollo who seeks to ransom his daughter.</note>, which means a man destined to pray to God. The Priests differed among themselves, as much by their functions as by the particular names given to them in various countries.

although since the time of **Homer** there were official Priests, such as **Chryses** and many others, the Kings, Princes, and leaders still performed sacrifices themselves. In several places, the Princes and Kings were themselves titled Priests; and even among those appointed to preside over the Mysteries, there was one in **Athens** who was called the <term>King</term> <note>original Greek: Βασιλεὺς (*Basileus*), a title given to the second of the nine archons who oversaw religious matters.</note>.

It seems that this custom had come from the **Jews**, who were commanded to exclude from priestly functions those who had any significant physical defects, such as being one-eyed, lame, etc. The **Athenians** also required of the Priests a pure and chaste life; the pleasures permitted to other men were forbidden to them. Within the order of the Roman Hierarchy, the Pontiffs were the foremost. At first, there were only four: but as this number was subsequently increased, they were distinguished into major Pontiffs and minor Pontiffs <note>original: *Pontifices majores* and *Pontifices minores*</note>. Both groups were subject to the Sovereign Pontiff <note>original: *Pontifex Maximus*</note>, whose authority was so great that the Emperors saw fit to unite this dignity with supreme power. As master of all the ceremonies of Religion and head of the first College <note>The College of Pontiffs, the most prestigious of the four major priestly colleges in Rome.</note>, the Sovereign Pontiff was held in extreme respect. His chariot, called the *Thensa* <term>Thensa: A highly ornamental ceremonial carriage, typically used to carry the images of the gods during sacred processions.</term>, was different from those of the other Priests, as was his attire and the rest of his equipage. He was not permitted to leave Italy; undoubtedly this law only bound the Sovereign Pontiff when he did not hold any other State Office alongside his religious dignity. Indeed, we see that Julius Caesar, after having been appointed Sovereign Pontiff, traveled to his governorship in Spain and subsequently to that of the Gauls, at a time when he was still subject to the laws, and without his enemies ever reproaching him for having broken them on that account.

In the order of the Roman Hierarchy, the Pontiffs were the first. At first, there were only four: but this number having been increased in the following years, they were distinguished into major Pontiffs and minor Pontiffs <note>original: *Pontifices majores* and *minores*. These were ranks within the College of Pontiffs, with the "major" pontiffs typically coming from the elite patrician class.</note>: both were subject to the Sovereign Pontiff <note>original: *Pontifex Maximus*, the high priest of the College of Pontiffs and the most important religious figure in ancient Rome.</note>, whose authority was so great that the Emperors judged it appropriate to unite this dignity with the supreme power. Master of all the ceremonies of Religion, and of the first College, the Sovereign Pontiff was extremely respected: his chariot, named *Thensa* <term>Thensa: A sacred, highly decorated carriage used to transport the images of the gods or the Sovereign Pontiff during religious processions.</term>, was different from that of the other Priests, as was his clothing and the rest of his equipment. He was not permitted to leave Italy; no doubt this Law only bound the Sovereign Pontiff when he did not join to his dignity any Office of the State; for we see that Julius Caesar, after having been created Sovereign Pontiff, traveled to his Government of Spain and then to that of Gaul, at a time when he was still subject to the Laws, and without his enemies ever reproaching him for having broken them for that reason.

Independently of these Ministers, the Greeks and Romans had others, who were also destined for the worship of the Gods, such as the **Augurs** <note>original: *Augures*; priests who sought to understand the will of the gods by observing the flight of birds.</note> and the **Haruspices** <note>original: *Aruſpices*; diviners who interpreted the will of the gods by inspecting the entrails of sacrificial animals.</note>, of whom I shall speak in the article on Divination.

As for the clothing of the various Priests and other Ministers mentioned in this Chapter, I refer the reader to the Antiquarians <note>Scholars of the early modern period who studied the physical remains and customs of antiquity.</note> who have had them drawn from ancient monuments. A simple inspection of these figures provides more information than the most detailed descriptions.

Here is the subject that led to the establishment of the *Apollonia* <note>A festival honoring Apollo, typically involving a procession to invite the god into the city.</note> by the people of *Aegialia* <note>An ancient name for the region of Sicyon in the Peloponnese.</note>. *Apollo*, after the defeat of *Python* <note>The monstrous serpent or dragon that Apollo slew at Delphi.</note>, retired to *Aegialia* with *Diana* <note>The author uses the Roman name for the Greek goddess Artemis.</note> his sister: but having been driven away, he was forced to go seek a retreat on the *Island of Crete*. However, as a plague was causing great ravages in the city that this God had just abandoned, they went to consult the *Oracle*, and learned that it was necessary to dispatch seven young boys and an equal number of young girls to seek *Apollo* and *Diana*, and bring them back home. This deputation pleased the two offended Divinities, and they returned to *Aegialia*, where a Temple was dedicated to *Peitho* <note>Original French: *Pitho*. She is the goddess of persuasion and seductive speech.</note>, Goddess of persuasion; and in memory of this event, the same number of boys and girls were sent out every year, as if to go in search of *Apollo* and *Diana*.

The *Carnea* <note>Original French: *Carnées*.</note>, mentioned by Herodotus (1) and Thucydides (1), were celebrated especially among the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans and their neighbors in the Laconia region.</note>, in honor of Apollo Carneus; and the *Caryae* <note>Original French: *Caries*.</note> in honor of Diana, surnamed *Caryatis* <note>Artemis Caryatis; the "caryatid" architectural columns are said to represent the young women who danced at this festival.</note>. The *Charitesia* <note>Original French: *Charities*.</note> were the Festival of the Graces. The *Cissotonia* <note>Original French: *Cissotonies*.</note>, so named from the ivy <note>From the Greek *kissos*, meaning ivy.</note> that was carried at this Festival, was instituted in honor of Hebe, Goddess of youth. The *Coreia* <note>Original French: *Corees*.</note> were the Festival of Proserpina, named *Core* <note>Original Greek: *Kore*, meaning "The Maiden."</note>. The *Corybantia* <note>Original French: *Corybantiques*.</note> were celebrated on the Island of Crete, in honor of the Corybantes <note>Armed and armored dancers who served the goddess Rhea or Cybele.</note>, of whom we will speak elsewhere. The *Kronia* <note>Original French: *Chronies*.</note>, celebrated in Athens in honor of Saturn <note>Known to the Greeks as Cronus.</note>, were nearly the same as the Saturnalia of the Romans. *Cynophontis* <note>Original French: *Cynophonie*.</note> was a Festival of Argos celebrated during the dog days <note>The hottest days of summer, associated with the rising of the Dog Star, Sirius.</note>, during which all dogs were killed; this gave the name to this Solemnity <note>From the Greek *kyon* (dog) and *phonos* (slaughter).</note>.

A copper Globe was placed on an olive branch, from which hung several other smaller globes: the first represented the Sun, or Apollo; the second, slightly smaller, represented the Moon; and the others, the Stars. The crowns surrounding these globes marked the days of the year. Roman Festivals always had some motive for their institution; the people asked the Gods for either a good harvest or some other blessing. They sought to appease those deities whom they believed they had offended; they wanted to turn away the evils with which they were threatened, as can be judged by the history of those I have just mentioned. Often, it was to remember a benefit received, and such was the festival named the ***Lucaria*** <note>original: *Luceries*</note>, a word derived from ***Lucus*** <note>the Latin word for a sacred wood or grove</note>. As the fear of future evils played a large part in the religious worship of the Pagans, they had established Festivals to be preserved from them: the one called *Robigalia* <note>the Festival of Mildew</note>, after the God *Robigus*, who was believed to protect the grain from rust <note>original: *rouille*; a fungal disease that could destroy wheat crops</note>, was among this number. It was celebrated at the end of April, and a sheep and a dog were offered to this Divinity, along with wine and incense.

The *Septimontium* <note>the Festival of the Seven Hills</note> was a Festival established in Rome when a seventh mountain was included within its boundaries. This Festival, during which seven sacrifices were offered in different places, fell in the month of December; and on that day, the Emperors would distribute gifts to the people.

Let us finish this list with the *Vinalia* <note>original: *Vinales*; festivals of wine</note>, which were celebrated twice a year: the 9th day before the Kalends of May <note>April 23rd</note>, and the 13th day before those of September <note>August 20th</note>. <margin>(2) Book 18, ch. 19.</margin> The first, established according to Pliny (2) to taste the wine, had no relation to the preservation of the vines; the second were intended to obtain a favorable time for the grape harvest.

Telles were the Festivals of the Romans, as marked in their Calendar; and if extraordinary ones were sometimes celebrated, such as the days destined for public Supplications <note>solemn rituals of prayer or thanksgiving decreed by the state during times of crisis or victory</note>, it was the Magistrate who indicated them in particular cases.

## CHAPTER XIV.
*On Public Supplications, Lectisternia, Evocations, and Devotions.*

Public <term>supplications</term> <note>solemn ceremonies of prayer or thanksgiving where the temples were opened to the public</note> were held either in pressing circumstances—such as during a time of plague or some widespread disease—or after some unexpected victory, when a newly elected General requested confirmation from the Senate along with a Supplication to make the Gods favorable, and for other reasons as well. These Supplications were solemn days during which it was not permitted to bring legal suits <note>original: *plaider*; the suspension of legal and public business was known as a *justitium*</note> for any reason whatsoever, and they were celebrated with Sacrifices, prayers, and public feasts. Sometimes the Senate limited the duration of this Festival to a single day; sometimes several days were spent on it, and History teaches us that there have been some that lasted up to fifty days.

Nothing is said of private Supplications, which were nothing more than

Valerius Maximus (1) makes mention of a <term>Lectisternium</term> <note>a sacred ritual where images of the gods were placed on couches and offered a symbolic meal</note> celebrated in honor of Jupiter. This God—that is to say, his statue—was reclined there upon a couch, while those of Juno and Mercury were placed on seats: *For at the banquet of Jupiter, he himself is invited to a small couch, while Juno and Mercury are invited to chairs for the dinner* <note>original Latin: "Nam Jovis épulo ipse in Lectulum, Juno & Mercurius in sellas ad coenam invitantur."</note>.

<margin>(2) Book 5, ch. 15.</margin>
Livy, Cicero, Lampridius, and others still speak often of this ceremony; and the first of these authors traces its institution to the year 354 of Rome <note>approximately 399 BCE</note> (2), on the occasion of the plague that was ravaging that city. This Lectisternium lasted eight days, and was celebrated in honor of Apollo, Latona, Diana, Hercules, Mercury, and Neptune. Valerius Maximus, in truth, mentions another even more ancient one, since according to him, it was celebrated under the consulship of Brutus and Valerius Poplicola <note>the first years of the Roman Republic, circa 509 BCE</note>: but apparently it was less solemn, or Livy was not aware of it.

Until the time of <term>Casaubon</term> <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a famous classical scholar who analyzed ancient texts</note>, it was believed that the Lectisternium was of Roman institution, and that it was not known outside of Italy: but this learned critic, examining a passage from the <term>Scholiast</term> <note>an ancient commentator or annotator of classical manuscripts</note> of

After what we have just said, it is evident that the <term>Lectisternium</term> <note>a ritual banquet where images of gods were placed on couches and offered a meal</note> was equally in use in Greece and in Italy. Let us add that the days destined for this Festival were among the most solemn, during which it was not permitted to send anyone to execution, and that even criminals were granted their freedom. It was the first Magistrate, or the Sovereign Pontiff <note>the *Pontifex Maximus*, the highest-ranking religious official in Rome</note> who announced these dates, and the objective was to appease the Gods or to ask them for certain favors. Let us finish by saying that the banquet table, and the beds where the Gods were to rest, were decorated with branches, flowers, and fragrant herbs. This is enough on this subject; let us say a word about Evocations.

I devote them by the authority of my office, for the Roman People, for our Army, and for our Legions, so that you may preserve both the Commanders and those who serve under their orders."

Antiquity has not preserved the formula for private <term>Devotions</term> <note>acts where an individual sacrificed themselves to the gods of the underworld to save the community</note> for us, but it is certain that one existed. When Decius <note>referring to Publius Decius Mus, a Roman consul who famously sacrificed himself in battle</note> devoted himself, he instructed—as I shall mention on another occasion—the <term>Pontiff</term> <note>a high-ranking priest in ancient Rome responsible for religious law</note> Valerius to pronounce the formula of Devotion: "Valerius," he said, "we have need of the help of the gods; proceed, and dictate the words by which I may devote myself for the Laws." <note>original Latin: *Deorum ope, Valeri, opus est; agendum, præverba quibus me pro Legibus devoveam.* While the text says "Laws," historical accounts of this event in Livy usually say "Legions" (*legionibus*).</note>

When the Law devoted someone to death, it was permitted to kill them. There was a law by Romulus <note>the legendary founder and first king of Rome</note> conceived in these terms: "If a Patron wrongs his Client, let him be accursed." <note>original Latin: *Si Patronus Clienti fraudem faxit, sacer esto.* The term *sacer esto* meant the person was "sacred" to the gods of the underworld, effectively making them an outlaw who could be killed without penalty.</note> If any <term>Patron</term> <note>a social superior who provided protection to a "Client" in exchange for loyalty and service</note> harms his Client, let him be devoted. It was to Pluto, or Dis, and to the other infernal Divinities <note>the gods who ruled the land of the dead</note>, that criminals were devoted.

I will say nothing here of the Supplications and Vows made by private individuals; one can easily see that the details of such things would be infinite.

<summary>This page concludes the Roman ritual formula for sacrificing enemies to the gods and explains how the concept of "devotion" applied to legal punishments and personal sacrifices for the state.</summary>
<keywords>devotio, Roman law, Decius Mus, ritual sacrifice, Pluto, Patron-Client relationship, sacer esto, infernal deities</keywords>

### C H A P T E R XV.

### *On Religious Ceremonies practiced at the foundation of Cities.*

I mentioned, a moment ago, that evocations <note>ritual summons intended to "call away" the protective gods of an enemy city to one's own side</note> were performed when a city was besieged, to invoke the gods under whose protection it was; and as these same gods became its patrons at the time of the foundation of each city, it is necessary to say a word about the ceremonies practiced on this occasion. Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian whose work is a major source for ancient Roman customs</note> informs us that the Etrurians <note>the Etruscans, a powerful civilization in ancient Italy that preceded and heavily influenced Roman religion and architecture</note> had books that contained the ceremonies used at the foundation of cities, altars, temples, walls, and gates; and Plutarch <note>a famous Greek biographer and philosopher</note> says that Romulus, wanting to lay the foundations of the city of Rome, sent for men from Etruria who taught him point by point all the ceremonies he was required to observe. According to Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>a Greek historian who lived in Rome and wrote a history of the city's early days</note>, they began by offering a sacrifice, after which they lit fires near the tents; and those who were to have some function in the construction of the city, lea-

<meta>catchword: lea- [from the French 'ſautoient,' meaning 'leaped' or 'jumped']</meta>

<summary>This page describes the religious origins of city-founding rituals, noting that the Romans adopted specific Etruscan ceremonies involving sacrifices and fire to ensure divine protection for their new walls and gates.</summary>

<page-num>565</page-num>

leaped over these fires <note>Continuing from the previous page, where it was mentioned that those participating in the city's construction jumped through fires</note> to purify themselves. Then they dug a pit into which they threw the first fruits of all things that served for human sustenance, as well as a handful of earth from the homeland of each person attending the ceremony.

At the same time, they consulted the gods to know if the enterprise would be pleasing to them, and if they approved of the day chosen to begin it. Next, they traced the perimeter with a trail of white earth, which was called *Pure Earth*; for want of this type of chalk, they used flour, as Alexander did, according to Strabo <note>a Greek geographer and historian who lived during the transition of the Roman Republic into the Empire</note>, when he laid the foundations of Alexandria. Once this first operation was finished, they opened a furrow as deep as possible with a bronze <term>airain: an archaic term usually referring to bronze or a similar copper alloy</term> plow, and they harnessed a white bull and a white heifer to this plow. All the space opened by the plow was considered holy. While they were forming the perimeter, they stopped from time to time to renew the sacrifices, and they marked the places where they were offered with a heap of stones called *Cippi* <note>original: "Cippes"; small pillars or boundary stones used as markers</note>. In these sacrifices, they invoked the gods under whose protection they

placed the new city, as well as the gods of the country, named *Native Ancestral Gods* <note>original: "Dii patrii Indigetes"</note>; this was done secretly, because the tutelary <note>guardian</note> gods of each city were supposed to remain unknown to the common people. Ovid, in his *Fasti* <note>a poetic treatise on the Roman calendar and its rituals</note>, has preserved for us the prayer formula that Romulus addressed to the gods whom he wished to make favorable to his enterprise.

> The King's voice spoke thus: "Jupiter, be present as I found the city,
> And father Mavors <note>an archaic name for Mars, the god of war</note>, and mother Vesta <note>goddess of the hearth</note>, be here.
> And all you gods whom it is pious to summon, take heed;
> With your blessing, may this work of mine rise," etc.
> <note>original Latin: "Vox fuit hæc Regis: Condenti Jupiter Urbem / Et genitor Mavors, Vestaque mater ades. / Quosque pium est adhibere Deos, advertite cuncti, / Auspicibus vobis hoc mihi surget opus, &c."</note>

Finally, the day of a city's foundation was held in such high regard that its memory was renewed in an annual festival; in Rome, this festival was the one called the *Parilia* <note>original: "Palilies"; a festival of purification and the birthday of Rome</note>, as we have already mentioned. Monsieur Blanchard, in a dissertation of which an extract is printed in the third volume of the *Memoirs of the Academy of Belles-Lettres* <margin>(1) Page 61.</margin> (1), explains the reasoning behind this ceremony and several others that do not have an essential connection to the pagan religion. Ovid has fortunately captured all these ceremonies in the <margin>(2) Fasti, book 4.</margin> following verses (2).

> A suitable day is chosen to mark the walls with the plow;
> The rites of Pales <note>the goddess of shepherds and livestock</note> were at hand: then the work began.
> <note>original Latin: "Apta dies legitur, qui mœnia signet aratro: / Sacra Palis suberant: inde movetur opus."</note>

*A pit is dug to solid ground, grains are cast into the bottom,*
*And earth is brought from neighboring soil.*
*The pit is filled with earth, and an altar is set upon the filled space,*
*And a new hearth is kindled as the fire blazes.*
*Then, pressing the plow-handle, he marks the walls with a furrow,*
*A white cow and a snow-white bull bore the yoke.*
<note>original Latin: "Fossa fit ad solidum, fruges jaciuntur in imâ, / Et de vicino terra petita solo. / Fossa repletur humo, plenæque imponitur ara, / Et novus accenso finditur igne focus. / Indè premens stivam designat mænia sulco, / Alba jugum niveo cum bove vacca tulit." — from Ovid's *Fasti*, Book IV, describing the ritual foundation of Rome.</note>

In this Book, we have seen the History of the origin and progress of Idolatry <note>in this historical context, "Idolatry" refers to the various systems of pagan polytheism</note>. I have spoken of matters concerning the worship <term>culte</term> <note>religious practice or devotion</note> offered to the Gods; of Temples, Altars, Sacrifices, Priests, and the Festivals that were celebrated in their honor, etc. There still remains to examine several important subjects regarding Idolatry, which I shall discuss in the following Book.
